He was scheduled for a follow-up visit in one month to monitor his blood pressure.Discussion: Hypertension is a global health problem that affects more than 1.13 billion people worldwide. It is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke, and kidney disease. In the United States alone, more than 45% of adults have hypertension. The prevalence of hypertension increases with age, affecting 75% of adults over the age of 60. Hypertension is defined as elevated blood pressure that is consistently above 140/90 mmHg. Hypertension is a chronic condition that requires long-term management with medications, lifestyle modifications, and regular follow-up visits with a healthcare provider. Lifestyle modifications that have been shown to be effective in managing hypertension include the DASH diet, salt reduction, physical activity, and maintaining a healthy weight. The DASH diet is rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and low-fat dairy products and has been shown to be effective in reducing blood pressure. Salt reduction has been shown to be effective in reducing blood pressure, especially in salt-sensitive individuals. Physical activity has been shown to be effective in reducing blood pressure, especially in individuals with systolic hypertension. Maintaining a healthy weight has been shown to be effective in reducing blood pressure, especially in overweight and obese individuals. In addition to lifestyle modifications, medications are often necessary to effectively manage hypertension. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are commonly used to manage hypertension. Calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers are also commonly used to manage hypertension. It is important for individuals with hypertension to regularly monitor their blood pressure and work closely with their healthcare provider to ensure that their blood pressure is well-controlled.

vignettes.prompt: Create a problem representation for a typical patient presenting with Hypertension, including complete demographic characterization and relevant past medical history
vignettes.response: Patients with hypertension typically present with elevated blood pressure (BP), commonly referred to as the “silent killer” due to the lack of apparent symptoms. The diagnosis of hypertension is made when systolic BP is greater than 140 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP is greater than 90 mm Hg (1). This condition may be further divided into prehypertension and hypertension. Prehypertension is characterized by systolic BP ranging from 120–139 mm Hg and diastolic BP ranging from 80–89 mm Hg, while hypertension is classified as Stage 1 (systolic BP of 140–159 mm Hg and diastolic BP of 90–99 mm Hg), Stage 2 (systolic BP of 160–179 mm Hg and diastolic BP of 100–109 mm Hg) or Stage 3 (systolic BP of 180 mm Hg or greater and/or diastolic BP of 110 mm Hg or greater) (1). Hypertension is a common condition, affecting over 30% of the adult population in the United States (2). The condition is more prevalent among African American populations and those with lower levels of education, while the prevalence of hypertension decreases with age (3, 4).

Case Report: 
 Hypertension (HTN) is a serious condition that affects over 60% of the world’s population and accounts for approximately 9.4 million deaths annually . It is estimated that by 2025, over 1.5 billion people will be diagnosed with HTN . HTN is the leading risk factor for cardiovascular disease, a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide . It is also a major risk factor for stroke, myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, and renal failure . HTN is a multifactorial disease, and the etiology and pathophysiology are not well understood. HTN is defined as elevated blood pressure (BP) greater than 140/90 mm Hg . The Joint National Committee on Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment of High Blood Pressure (JNC-7) report classifies HTN as: normal BP (systolic BP <120 mm Hg and diastolic BP <80 mm Hg), prehypertension (systolic BP of 120-139 mm Hg or diastolic BP of 80-89 mm Hg), and stage 1 HTN (systolic BP of 140-159 mm Hg or diastolic BP of 90-99 mm Hg) and stage 2 HTN (systolic BP of ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic BP of ≥100 mm Hg) . The incidence of HTN increases with age, with the prevalence being lower in young adults than in older adults. The prevalence of HTN in older adults is 50-80% .

vignettes.response: INTRODUCTION: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycemia due to defects in insulin secretion, insulin resistance, or both . Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is an autoimmune disease that causes insulin deficiency in the pancreas, whereas type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a metabolic disease characterized by insulin resistance in the liver, muscle, and adipose tissue . In T1DM, the autoimmune process causes the destruction of insulin-producing beta cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency and requiring lifelong insulin therapy . His home medications included glipizide 5 mg daily, metformin 850 mg daily, and insulin aspart 6 units before meals and 12 units before bedtime. The patient was started on intravenous insulin infusion and was monitored closely in the intensive care unit for volume management and hypoglycemia prevention. His insulin regimen was adjusted according to his blood glucose levels. The patient's blood glucose was monitored every hour, and insulin infusion was adjusted according to his blood glucose level. vignettes.response: Preeclampsia is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy that can occur in any pregnant woman. It is a serious condition that can lead to severe complications for both the mother and the baby, including seizures, stroke, kidney failure, and death. It is a condition that is usually diagnosed after 20 weeks of pregnancy, and it can occur in any pregnancy, including primiparas and multiparas. The most common symptoms of preeclampsia are high blood pressure and proteinuria, but it can also cause headaches, visual disturbances, upper abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and pulmonary edema. The risk factors for preeclampsia are unknown, but it is more likely to occur in women who have had preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy, have chronic hypertension, diabetes, autoimmune disorders, kidney disease, and family history of preeclampsia. It is also more likely to occur in women who are over 40 years old, have a multiple pregnancy, and have a history of other pregnancy complications such as infections, in vitro fertilization, and recurrent miscarriages. The diagnosis of preeclampsia is usually based on the new onset of hypertension and proteinuria after 20 weeks of pregnancy. The blood pressure must be equal or greater than 140/90 mmHg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart. Proteinuria can be detected by a urine dipstick test, which measures the amount of protein in the urine. A positive test is when the urine test shows 1+ or greater, which is equivalent to 30 mg of protein per deciliter of urine. The treatment of preeclampsia includes managing the high blood pressure, reducing proteinuria, preventing seizures, and delivering the baby and the placenta. The only cure for preeclampsia is delivery. Therefore, it is essential to identify preeclampsia early and manage it appropriately to prevent severe complications for the mother and the baby.

vignettes.response: Preeclampsia is a potentially life-threatening pregnancy-specific complication that develops during or after pregnancy . The estimated prevalence of preeclampsia ranges from 2% to 8% of all pregnancies . The onset of preeclampsia is usually after 20 weeks of gestation and symptoms may appear suddenly, or a gradual onset may occur. The symptoms include severe headaches, elevated blood pressure, edema, abdominal pain, visual disturbances, nausea, vomiting, and sudden weight gain . Preeclampsia is a severe condition that can lead to organ failure, seizures, and death. The condition is defined as elevated blood pressure with signs of dysfunction of one or more organs, and signs of hypertension and proteinuria occurring after 20 weeks of gestation .

vignettes.prompt: Create a problem representation for a typical patient presenting with Preeclampsia, including complete demographic characterization and relevant past medical history
vignettes.response: Preeclampsia is a serious condition that can develop during pregnancy, and it is characterized by high blood pressure and high protein levels in the urine after 20 weeks of pregnancy. Preeclampsia affects 2% to 8% of all pregnancies globally and is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity . The exact cause of preeclampsia is unknown, but it is thought to involve problems with the placenta, immune system, and genetic factors. The condition can be life-threatening for both the mother and the baby, and it is important to receive prompt medical attention if you experience symptoms. Common symptoms of preeclampsia include high blood pressure, swelling in the face and hands, weight gain, headaches, upper abdominal pain, vision changes, and sudden weight gain. Other symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, fever, and sudden weight gain. It is important to seek medical help immediately if you experience any of these symptoms, especially if you are pregnant. Preeclampsia can be treated with medication and in some cases, the baby may need to be delivered. However, the best course of action will depend on the specific circumstances of the patient. It is important to work closely with your healthcare provider to develop a treatment plan that is right for you.

Title: Severe Preeclampsia in a Primiparous Patient with a History of Chronic Hypertension and Gestational Hypertension

Patient Background: A 26-year-old, gravida 1, para 0, Hispanic female, with a history of chronic hypertension and gestational hypertension, presented to the obstetric triage unit at 34 weeks of gestation with complaints of blurred vision, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain. Her blood pressure was 175/110 mmHg, and she had 3+ proteinuria on urinalysis. A fetal heart rate monitor revealed a non-reactive fetal heart pattern, with no significant decelerations or bradycardia. A complete blood count was normal, and liver and renal function were within normal limits. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the head showed no acute intracranial pathology. A fetal ultrasound revealed oligohydramnios, a normal amniotic fluid index, and normal fetal growth. A placental ultrasound showed a thickened placenta with no evidence of low-lying placenta or placental previa. A maternal 24-hour urine protein level was 4.12 g/day. The patient was diagnosed with severe preeclampsia with severe features. Her blood pressure was managed with intravenous hydralazine and labetalol, and her proteinuria was treated with intravenous magnesium sulfate. The patient was admitted to the labor and delivery unit for delivery of the baby and placental pathology evaluation. The patient was consented for a possible cesarean delivery and placental biopsy. A cesarean delivery was performed, and the patient had a normal spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 2.84 kg male infant with Apgar scores of 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. The patient had an uncomplicated postpartum course, and was discharged home on postpartum day 3. Placental biopsy revealed extensive fibrin deposition with no evidence of infarction or vasculopathy. The placental biopsy was consistent with early-onset preeclampsia. The patient was seen in the outpatient clinic at 6 weeks postpartum and was doing well. Follow-up at 3 months revealed that the patient was normotensive and had no proteinuria, and that her infant had normal growth and development.

vignettes.response: Case Title: A 38-Year-Old Pregnant Patient Presenting with Preeclampsia and HELLP SyndromeCase Background: A 38-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presented to the emergency department with severe headaches and blurred vision for three days. She also complained of nausea, vomiting, and upper abdominal pain. The patient had a history of asthma and pre-eclampsia during her first pregnancy. The patient was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia at 28 weeks of gestation in this pregnancy and was treated with labetalol and magnesium sulfate. She was also diagnosed with gestational diabetes and was being treated with insulin.Case Report: The patient was admitted to the hospital and was found to have a blood pressure of 170/110 mmHg with a pulse rate of 110 beats per minute. Her fundal height was consistent with her 32 weeks of gestation. On physical examination, the patient had a 3/6 systolic murmur over the aorta. The laboratory workup was significant for a white blood cell count of 15,000 cells/mm3, hemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL, platelet count of 62,000 cells/mm3, creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL, and aspartate transaminase (AST) of 366 IU/L. The urine analysis showed 2+ proteinuria, and the urine eosinophil count was 20/high power field. The patient was diagnosed with HELLP syndrome and was given three units of packed red blood cells and a transfusion of two units of fresh frozen plasma. The patient was also given magnesium sulfate and was placed on an insulin drip. The patient was started on intravenous methyldopa and labetalol. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit due to worsening hypoxia. The patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and she was eventually intubated. The patient subsequently developed disseminated intravascular coagulation, and she underwent an emergency cesarean section. The patient delivered a live male infant with a birth weight of 1,700 g. The patient was discharged from the hospital on postoperative day 12.Case Significance: This case highlights the importance of recognizing the signs and symptoms of preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome. Preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome are major causes of maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality. Early recognition and prompt treatment are crucial for improving outcomes.

Title: Uncontrolled HIV with Cerebral Toxoplasmosis: A Case Report 
 Author: [Your Name]  Abstract: We present a case of a 30-year-old male with a history of HIV, cryptococcal meningitis, and an ongoing hospitalization for a complicated course of cryptococcal meningitis who developed cerebral toxoplasmosis. We discuss the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of cerebral toxoplasmosis in patients with HIV and cryptococcal meningitis.  Introduction: Cerebral toxoplasmosis is a rare but serious complication of HIV infection. It is caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii, which can cause damage to the brain and central nervous system. Cerebral toxoplasmosis can present with a variety of symptoms, including headache, seizures, confusion, and cognitive impairment.  Case presentation: We present the case of a 30-year-old male who was diagnosed with HIV and cryptococcal meningitis in 2019. He was admitted to the hospital for a complicated course of cryptococcal meningitis, which included several readmissions and changes in his antifungal therapy. During his latest admission, he developed a fever and altered mental status. He was found to have cerebral toxoplasmosis on MRI of the brain, which was confirmed by a positive Toxoplasma gondii PCR from a lumbar puncture. He was treated with sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, and folinic acid. He was discharged after a two-week hospitalization and has since been lost to follow-up.  Discussion: Cerebral toxoplasmosis is a serious complication of HIV infection. It is caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii, which can cause damage to the brain and central nervous system. Symptoms can include headache, seizures, confusion, and cognitive impairment. Diagnosis is typically made through a combination of clinical symptoms, MRI of the brain, and a Toxoplasma gondii PCR. Treatment typically involves a combination of anti-parasitic medication and anti-inflammatory agents. The prognosis for cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV patients can be poor, with a mortality rate of up to 50%. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential for the best chance of recovery.  Conclusion: Cerebral toxoplasmosis is a serious complication of HIV infection that can cause significant morbidity and mortality. It is important for healthcare providers to be aware of the signs and symptoms of cerebral toxoplasmosis and to consider it in the differential diagnosis of HIV patients presenting with neurological symptoms. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential for the best chance of recovery.

vignettes.response: Title: HIV-associated Kaposi Sarcoma and SARS-CoV-2 Infection: A Case Report and Literature Review.1. Introduction: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a neoplasm of vascular and lymphoid endothelial cells. It was originally described in 1872 and was named after its discoverer, Dr. Moritz Kaposi, a Hungarian dermatologist. KS was initially considered rare, however, in the 1980s, a significant increase in the incidence of KS was noted among men who have sex with men (MSM), particularly those infected with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). HIV-associated KS is the most common form of KS in the United States. In the pre-antiretroviral therapy (ART) era, 1 in 3 patients with AIDS had KS. The incidence of KS has decreased with the use of ART, but it remains a common AIDS-defining illness . In the current era, KS is now considered an HIV-associated malignancy. It is a neoplasm of vascular and lymphoid endothelial cells and is associated with the human herpes virus 8 (HHV-8). HIV-associated KS is more common in males than females, with a median age of 37 years. KS is usually a cutaneous disease, but it can also involve the viscera, lymph nodes, and oral cavity. In the current case, we present a 55-year-old male who developed a rapidly progressing KS of the head and neck region along with a new onset of shortness of breath and cough. He was found to be positive for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection.2. Case Report: A 55-year-old male with a past medical history of HIV, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented to the emergency room with a one-week history of a non-pruritic, non-tender, dark-red rash involving his head, neck, and upper chest. vignettes.response: Case 1: A 48-year-old male patient with a history of HIV infection and ART treatment presented to the emergency room (ER) with altered mental status. The patient was able to provide a history of anorexia, weight loss, and increased weakness over the past three months. The patient's recent laboratory results showed a CD4 count of 11 cells/mm3. The patient was diagnosed with HIV one year ago and was started on antiretroviral therapy. However, he was lost to follow-up and did not seek care for over a year. Upon arrival to the ER, the patient was ill-appearing, with a temperature of 101.8 F, pulse of 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 132/68 mmHg. On physical examination, the patient was lethargic, with poor dentition, and a tongue with oral thrush. The patient's lungs were clear on auscultation, and his heart and abdomen were normal on examination. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 12 (E4V2M6). He was intubated and started on norepinephrine. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count (WBC) of 3.7 K/mm3 with 65% neutrophils, hemoglobin of 10.1 g/dL, and platelets of 193 K/mm3. The patient's sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, and glucose levels were within the normal range. Creatinine was elevated at 1.9 mg/dL, and the patient had an anion gap of 25. Lactate levels were not obtained. Liver function tests showed aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 79 U/L and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 84 U/L, with a total bilirubin level of 0.9 mg/dL. The patient's HIV viral load was 28,849 copies/mL, and the CD4 count was 3 cells/mm3. The patient's initial CT head showed no acute intracranial process. A lumbar puncture was performed, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed a white blood cell count of 12 cells/mm3 with 90% lymphocytes, glucose level of 36 mg/dL, and protein level of 64 mg/dL. The patient was diagnosed with HIV-associated meningoencephalitis and was started on empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, including vancomycin and ceftriaxone. The patient was also started on acyclovir for suspected herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis. The patient was extubated on hospital day 14 and discharged to a rehabilitation facility on hospital day 19. The patient's antibiotics were discontinued on hospital day 23. The patient was readmitted to the hospital on hospital day 29 due to worsening mental status, and a repeat CT head showed acute hydrocephalus. The patient underwent placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, and his mental status improved. The patient was discharged home on hospital day 35 and has since been followed up in the outpatient setting.

vignettes.prompt: Compose a brief presentation of a patient presenting with Tuberculosis. Please include complete demographic information and past medical history.
vignettes.response: Good morning everyone, today I would like to present a case of tuberculosis. Tuberculosis, or TB, is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It typically affects the lungs but can also affect other organs such as the brain, spine, and kidneys. It is a major global health problem, with an estimated 10 million cases and 1.4 million deaths occurring annually. The disease can be spread through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People who are in close contact with someone who has TB are at higher risk of becoming infected. Symptoms of TB include coughing for more than three weeks, coughing up blood, weight loss, fever, night sweats, and fatigue.

vignettes.response: Good morning everyone. Today, I would like to present a case of a 45-year-old male patient who presented to our clinic with a two-week history of cough, fever, and fatigue. The patient is a farmer by profession and a non-smoker. He has no history of tuberculosis in the past and does not have any family history of tuberculosis. His chest examination revealed vesicular breathing with bilateral basal crepitations. His abdominal examination was normal. His neurological and joint examinations were also normal. His initial workup included a complete blood count, which showed leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 11,500 cells per microliter. His hemoglobin was 11.5 g/dL. His renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. His erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 80 mm/hr. His chest X-ray (Figure 1) and CT scan (Figure 2) of the chest showed bilateral lower zone consolidation with cavitation. His sputum was collected and sent for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) staining, and the sample was sent for GeneXpert. The patient was started on anti-tubercular treatment (ATT). He was given isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for four months. His cough improved after two weeks of starting ATT. The patient was followed up after two weeks, and his repeat chest X-ray showed improvement (Figure 3). His repeat complete blood count showed a white blood cell count of 9,000 cells per microliter, and his ESR was 40 mm/hr. His sputum sample was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis by GeneXpert. In conclusion, this patient presented with symptoms of tuberculosis and had a positive sputum culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He was started on ATT, and his symptoms improved after two weeks.

vignettes.prompt: Create a problem representation for a typical patient presenting with Tuberculosis, including complete demographic characterization and relevant past medical history
vignettes.response: Problem Representation: Tuberculosis (TB) is a communicable disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It commonly affects the lungs and causes symptoms such as cough, chest pain, and fever. The disease is transmitted through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. He was initially diagnosed with pneumonia and was prescribed antibiotics but his symptoms did not improve. He then developed a productive cough, yellow sputum, and hemoptysis. He also complained of chest pain, fatigue, and weight loss of 10 pounds over the past month. He denied any history of smoking, drug abuse, or exposure to contagious diseases. He had a history of tuberculosis (TB) infection three years prior that was treated with a nine-month course of antituberculosis medication. Upon physical examination, he was febrile with a temperature of 101°F and had decreased breath sounds at the left lung base. His white blood cell count was 11,000 cells/mm3, and his hemoglobin level was 10.8 g/dL. A chest radiograph revealed a right hilar mass and a left lower lobe opacity (Figure 1). A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest confirmed a 4.5 cm hilar mass and a 2.5 cm left lower lobe nodule (Figure 2). The CT scan also revealed extensive necrotic lymph nodes, some as large as 2.5 cm. A bronchoscopy was performed, which showed normal upper airways and an inflamed trachea. Biopsies were taken from the tracheal inflammation, and the pathology results were inconclusive. A biopsy of the left lower lobe nodule was performed, which revealed necrotic material with acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on smear and tuberculous granulomas on pathology (Figure 3). AFB cultures were positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A QuantiFERON test was also positive. The patient was diagnosed with multidrug-resistant (MDR) tuberculosis and was started on a regimen of bedaquiline, clofazimine, linezolid, and cycloserine. After one month of treatment, the patient's cough had subsided, and his fever and fatigue had resolved. A follow-up chest CT scan revealed a decrease in size of the hilar mass and the left lower lobe nodule (Figure 4). The patient is currently in stable condition and continues antituberculosis treatment.

vignettes.prompt: Create a case report about a patient with Tuberculosis. A good case report description includes complete demographic information as well as past medical history.
vignettes.response: Patient information: A 65-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital on 13 February 2021 due to a cough that had persisted for over half a year. The patient had no other symptoms of fever, chest pain, or phlegm production. The patient had a history of hypertension for five years and was taking antihypertensive drugs regularly. She denied any family history of genetic disease or any history of close contact with patients with tuberculosis. Physical examination: The patient had normal vital signs. Cardiopulmonary auscultation revealed scattered breath sounds in both lungs. No abnormalities were found in the remainder of the physical examination. Laboratory examination: Routine blood test results were normal. The liver and kidney function tests were normal. The C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 5.2 mg/L (normal range 0–10 mg/L), and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 120 mm/h (normal range 0–20 mm/h). The sputum culture showed no pathogens. Chest CT scan: Chest CT scan revealed multiple nodules in the right upper, middle, and lower lobes of the lung, with a few irregular patchy shadowing around the nodules, and multiple nodules with irregular shapes were seen in the left lower lobe of the lung, which were distributed around the bronchus (Figures 1A–1D). The imaging features were highly suggestive of tuberculosis. Sputum smear and culture: The sputum smear was positive for acid-fast bacilli, and the sputum culture was positive for M. tuberculosis. Pulmonary function test: The pulmonary function test showed that the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) was 2.00 L, the forced vital capacity (FVC) was 3.07 L, and the FEV1/FVC was 66.27%. Bronchoscopy: Bronchoscopy revealed that the bronchial mucosa was congested and edematous, the mucosa was slightly thickened, and the mucosal epithelium was slightly eroded, with hyperemia. Transbronchial lung biopsy: The results of transbronchial lung biopsy showed that the alveolar septa were thickened and deformed, the alveolar spaces were fused, and there was lymphocytic and monocytic interstitial infiltration, and the alveolar walls were infiltrated with a small amount of lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). Pathological diagnosis: Pathological diagnosis showed granulomatous inflammation, necrosis, and caseous necrosis, which were consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis. Treatment and follow-up: The patient was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and was given anti-tuberculosis treatment with a combination of rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. The patient’s cough and sputum production were significantly reduced after one week of treatment, and the cough completely disappeared after two weeks of treatment. The patient was followed up for six months, and chest CT re-examination showed that the lesions in both lungs were significantly absorbed, and the imaging findings were significantly improved (Figures 1E–1H).

The patient reports a decreased appetite, night sweats, and fatigue over the past month. He also reports shortness of breath but denies chest pain, coughing up blood, and difficulty breathing. He reports no history of prior tuberculosis testing or treatment. The patient reports a history of hepatitis B vaccination. Physical exam is remarkable for tachycardia and tachypnea, with a temperature of 39.6°C. Chest exam reveals diminished breath sounds at the right lung base. Labs are remarkable for leukocytosis (16.8 x 103/uL), lymphopenia (0.6 x 103/uL), anemia (9.8 g/dL), elevated ESR (120 mm/hr), and a normal LDH. The patient is monitored closely with regular follow-up visits and repeat chest radiographs at 2 and 6 months, which show resolution of the lesion.Tuberculosis, or TB, is a bacterial infection caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. It typically affects the lungs (pulmonary TB) but can also affect other organs, such as the brain, kidneys, and spine (extrapulmonary TB). TB is spread through the air when people with active TB cough or sneeze, releasing droplets that contain the bacteria into the air. People with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV, are at a higher risk of developing TB. The symptoms of TB can vary depending on the location of the infection, but may include cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats, and shortness of breath. Diagnosis of TB typically involves a combination of clinical symptoms, chest X-ray, and laboratory testing such as a tuberculin skin test or sputum culture. Treatment of TB usually involves taking multiple antibiotics for several months. It is important for medical students to be familiar with TB and its presentation, as it is a common and potentially deadly disease that is treatable with antibiotics.

The biopsy showed noncaseating granuloma formation, and the diagnosis of sarcoidosis was made (Figure 2). The patient was started on prednisone 40 mg daily. His past medical history was significant for asthma and hypertension. His family history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds in the left lung and diminished breath sounds in the right lung. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. Diagnosis of sarcoidosis is made based on clinical presentation, radiographic findings, and biopsy of affected tissues. Treatment of sarcoidosis involves corticosteroids, which can help reduce symptoms and prevent progression of the disease. Prognosis of sarcoidosis depends on the extent of organ involvement and response to treatment.

vignettes.response: "This 43-year-old African American male with a past medical history of hyperlipidemia, asthma, and Sarcoidosis presented with a 3-month history of cough and shortness of breath that progressed to include fevers, chills, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. He was started on prednisone 40 mg daily with improvement in his symptoms and PFTs improved to a baseline FVC of 2.3 L (78%) and FEV1 of 2.1 L (85%). He was weaned off prednisone and remained asymptomatic for a year until presenting with worsening cough and dyspnea and a repeat CXR showing progressive pulmonary infiltrates and nodules. Repeat CT scan of the chest revealed new pleural effusions with a loculated right pleural effusion (Figure 2) and positive sputum AFB culture growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He was diagnosed with pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and started on antituberculosis therapy with rifampin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. His symptoms improved, and he was started on prednisone 40 mg daily with resolution of his pleural effusions and improvement in his PFTs. He is currently stable and continuing on antituberculosis therapy and prednisone."

A bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsies of the nodules was performed. Histologic examination revealed noncaseating granulomas, and mycobacterial and fungal stains were negative (Figure 3). The patient was referred to an infectious disease specialist, who ordered a QuantiFERON test, tuberculin skin test, and blood cultures. All the tests were negative. A pulmonology consultation was made, and the patient was started on prednisone 50 mg daily and an inhaler with budesonide and formoterol. The cough and chest pain improved within 2 weeks, and the patient was referred for a follow-up chest CT scan, which showed significant improvement in the size of the nodules (Figures 4, 5). The patient was monitored with a pulmonology follow-up every 3 months for the next 2 years. He remained asymptomatic, and his chest CT scan showed no evidence of disease activity.Discussion: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disease of unknown etiology characterized by noncaseating granulomas. The pathogenesis of sarcoidosis is unclear, but it is believed to involve an abnormal immune response to an antigen or infectious agent. Sarcoidosis can affect any organ, but the lungs are involved in up to 90% of cases. The most common presentation of pulmonary sarcoidosis is a bilateral reticulonodular pattern on chest radiograph, which can be confused with pulmonary tuberculosis. Other radiologic findings include hilar lymphadenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, and pulmonary nodules. The diagnosis of sarcoidosis is based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on biopsy and exclusion of other causes of granulomatous disease, including tuberculosis. The treatment of sarcoidosis depends on the extent and severity of the disease. Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment for sarcoidosis, but their efficacy is limited, and relapses are common after cessation of therapy. Other immunosuppressive agents, such as methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine, may be used in patients who do not respond to corticosteroids or have severe disease.Problem-based learning (PBL) is a pedagogical approach that has gained increasing popularity in medical education over the past few decades. PBL is a student-centered learning approach that encourages students to take responsibility for their own learning and develop critical thinking skills. It has been shown to be effective in improving student learning outcomes, such as knowledge acquisition and problem-solving skills, and promoting student motivation and engagement in the learning process. In this study, we explored the feasibility of using PBL to teach medical students about sarcoidosis, a rare and complex disease. We developed a PBL case focused on a young patient with sarcoidosis and delivered it to a group of medical students. We found that the students were highly engaged in the PBL session and demonstrated a better understanding of the disease after the session. We also found that the PBL approach was feasible to implement and did not require significant additional resources or time. Based on these findings, we recommend the use of PBL as a teaching strategy to improve students' knowledge and understanding of sarcoidosis.

The incidence of syphilis has been on the rise in recent years, particularly among men who have sex with men.Case Report: A 32-year-old male presented with a one-month history of a painless rash on his trunk and extremities. The rash began as multiple pink papules that coalesced over time to form a scaly plaque. He also noted swollen lymph nodes in his groin and neck. His CD4+ T-cell count was 364 cells/mm3, and HIV RNA was undetectable. Syphilis serology showed a reactive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test and a positive treponemal antibody test (T. pallidum particle agglutination assay, TP-PA). The patient was diagnosed with early disseminated syphilis and was treated with intramuscular penicillin G benzathine (2.4 MU) once weekly for three weeks. His rash resolved within two weeks of treatment, and his lymph nodes resolved within one month.Conclusion: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease that can present with a wide range of manifestations. vignettes.response: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection that can be transmitted from mother to child during pregnancy. The disease is caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum and is classified as an STI due to its sexual transmission. It can also be transmitted through blood transfusions, organ transplants, and sharing needles or syringes with an infected person. Syphilis is divided into four stages: primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary. The primary stage is characterized by a chancre, a painless sore that develops at the site of inoculation. The secondary stage is characterized by a rash, swollen lymph nodes, and potentially life-threatening complications such as meningitis and stroke. The latent stage can last for years or decades and may not be noticeable, but complications can still occur during this stage. The tertiary stage is divided into three phases: late neurosyphilis, late osteoarticular syphilis, and late gummatous syphilis.

vignettes.response: Syphilis is a chronic, systemic, sexually transmitted disease caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. It is spread through sexual contact, including vaginal, anal, and oral sex. Although rare, syphilis can also be transmitted from mother to baby during pregnancy, or through blood transfusions. The incubation period of syphilis is 10 to 90 days, depending on the stage of the disease. After an incubation period, syphilis progresses through four stages: primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary. The primary stage of syphilis is characterized by a painless chancre that develops at the site of inoculation. The secondary stage is characterized by a skin rash, mucosal lesions, condylomata lata, and lymphadenopathy. The latent stage of syphilis has no clinical symptoms but is still infectious. The tertiary stage of syphilis is characterized by cardiovascular, neurologic, ophthalmic, and musculoskeletal manifestations.

Title: A Case of Early Disseminated Syphilis in a Young Adult Female Patient

Patient is a 24-year-old female, presented to the outpatient clinic with a non-pruritic maculopapular rash on her back, abdomen, and limbs, for the past 2 months. She had no associated symptoms such as fever, chills, body pain, oral ulcers, genital ulcers, joint pain, lymphadenopathy, weight loss, or dyspnea. She denied any recent travel history, history of blood transfusions, tattoos, body piercings, or sexual contact. She denied any history of sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) and had no history of any other chronic illnesses. Patient denied any history of drug abuse, and her family history was unremarkable. She was on no regular medications. Patient had normal vital signs on presentation, and she was afebrile. On physical examination, she had a non-pruritic maculopapular rash on her back, abdomen, and limbs. The rash was erythematous and slightly raised and was not tender on palpation. There was no scarring or pigmentary changes associated with the rash. She had no oral ulcers, genital ulcers, or lymphadenopathy on examination. Laboratory tests were significant for a positive VDRL test, with a titer of 1:64, and a reactive Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay (TPPA) test. She had a normal complete blood count, renal function, liver function, and urinalysis. A chest X-ray and electrocardiogram were unremarkable. The patient was diagnosed with early disseminated syphilis and was started on aqueous crystalline penicillin G, 2 million units intravenously every 4 hours for 14 days. At the 3-month follow-up visit, the patient was asymptomatic with no skin rash, and a repeat VDRL test was negative.

vignettes.response: Sure, here is a brief case report that you may consider using for training medical students on Syphilis:Title: Syphilis in a young female patientCase presentationA 23-year-old woman presented to the emergency room with a 2-week history of a painless, slowly enlarging sore on the side of her vagina. She also complained of a sore throat, fever, swollen lymph nodes, and fatigue. She had no history of sexually transmitted infections and was in a monogamous relationship. She had not recently traveled or received blood transfusions. On physical examination, the patient was febrile (101°F), and a 1-cm ulcer was noted on the right posterior labia, with erythema and induration extending to the left labia. A swollen, tender lymph node was palpated in the right groin. A monofilament test was positive for chlamydia and gonorrhea, but the results were negative for syphilis. She was diagnosed with secondary syphilis based on the presence of a painless ulcer and systemic symptoms. She was treated with penicillin G benzathine (2.4 MU IM) and doxycycline (100 mg orally twice a day for 14 days), and her symptoms resolved.DiscussionSyphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. It is divided into three stages: primary, secondary, and latent. The primary stage is characterized by a chancre, which is a painless ulcer that appears 10 to 90 days after infection. The secondary stage is characterized by a rash, mucosal lesions, lymphadenopathy, and systemic symptoms such as fatigue, headache, and fever. The latent stage is asymptomatic and can last for years or decades before reactivation. Syphilis can cause serious complications if left untreated, including cardiovascular disease, neurosyphilis, and death.The diagnosis of syphilis is based on clinical presentation, laboratory tests, and a history of exposure. The primary and secondary stages can be diagnosed with dark-field microscopy, which is a specialized technique that allows the visualization of Treponema pallidum. In the primary stage, dark-field microscopy can detect spirochetes in the chancre. In the secondary stage, dark-field microscopy can detect spirochetes in mucosal lesions, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and bone marrow. In the latent stage, dark-field microscopy is not useful. Serologic tests are used to diagnose syphilis in the latent stage and can also be used to diagnose the primary and secondary stages. A positive Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test or Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay indicates an immune response to the infection. vignettes.response: Prostate cancer is the most common malignancy in men over the age of 50 years and the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States . The presentation of prostate cancer is typically asymptomatic in its early stages, with symptoms only appearing in advanced disease. The most common symptoms of prostate cancer include urinary incontinence, dysuria, pelvic pain, and weight loss. Diagnosis is typically made through a combination of physical examination, blood tests, and imaging. The prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test is a commonly used screening tool for prostate cancer, but it is not specific for the disease and can be elevated in other conditions, such as benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and prostatitis. Imaging techniques such as ultrasound, MRI, and PET can also be used to diagnose prostate cancer. Treatment options for prostate cancer include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, androgen deprivation therapy, and active surveillance. The choice of treatment depends on several factors, including the stage and grade of the cancer, the patient's age and overall health, and the patient's preferences.

The transrectal ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to produce images of the prostate. If any of these tests are abnormal, the doctor may recommend a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis.

vignettes.response: Prostate cancer is a common malignancy in men and is associated with high morbidity and mortality rates worldwide. Prostate cancer is the second most common cause of cancer-related death in men after lung cancer . The most common symptom of prostate cancer is urinary retention, which can lead to urinary tract infections and renal failure. Other symptoms include dysuria, hematuria, and constipation. Diagnosis of prostate cancer is often done with a digital rectal examination (DRE), prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test, and transrectal ultrasound (TRUS). Treatment options for prostate cancer include watchful waiting, surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and hormone therapy. The choice of treatment depends on several factors, including the stage of the cancer, the patient's age and overall health, and the patient's preferences. In this case report, we present a patient with advanced prostate cancer who underwent palliative surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy.

He was admitted to a local hospital, and a biopsy was done which confirmed that his prostate cancer had recurred. The tumor was locally advanced, and he was advised for chemotherapy. However, he refused the chemotherapy and left against medical advice. His urinary symptoms continued to worsen, and he developed urinary retention. He had to catheterize himself to empty his bladder. A CT scan of his abdomen and pelvis showed a large prostate mass with local invasion of the seminal vesicles and bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis. A cystoscopy showed a 5 cm × 5 cm prostate mass encasing the urethra, which was biopsied. The biopsy confirmed the recurrence of prostate cancer. Diagnosis:Recurrent prostate cancer with locally advanced disease. Management:His urinary symptoms were managed by inserting a Foley's catheter. He was started on antibiotics to prevent urinary tract infections. His chemotherapy was started under the oncologist's care. He responded well to the chemotherapy and underwent a second radical prostatectomy. His postoperative course was uneventful. He was discharged on oral antibiotics and analgesics. He was advised to continue his follow-up with his oncologist and urologist.

He has also noticed a small amount of blood in his urine for the past week. He denies any pain or difficulty initiating a stream. He does have a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, which are all well-controlled with medication. He also has a history of smoking 1 pack per day for 30 years, which he quit 20 years ago. He denies any history of allergies or family history of prostate or other cancers.Physical exam: The patient is in no acute distress. Vital signs are within normal limits, and he is well-hydrated. Abdominal exam is negative for tenderness or costovertebral angle tenderness. Cardiac and pulmonary exam are normal. On genitourinary exam, the prostate is enlarged and irregular on DRE. No nodules or masses are appreciated. The external genitalia and urethral meatus look normal. The bladder is full on digital rectal exam, and there is a trace of blood at the external os. A PSA level is drawn and sent for analysis.The patient is diagnosed with prostate cancer and scheduled for a prostate biopsy.Possible discussion points:• Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men in the United States.• The incidence of prostate cancer in the United States is around 175,000 new cases per year, with around 32,000 deaths per year.• The incidence of prostate cancer is highest in African American men and lowest in Asian men.• The incidence of prostate cancer peaks in men in their late 60s to early 70s.• Prostate cancer is often asymptomatic in its early stages.• The most common presenting symptom of prostate cancer is difficulty urinating.• The PSA test is a common screening test for prostate cancer, but it is not perfect.• A normal PSA level is typically under 4 ng/mL.• A PSA level above 4 ng/mL is considered abnormal and can indicate prostate cancer, but there are many other things that can cause an elevated PSA level, such as urinary tract infections, prostatitis, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), or prostate cancer.• A digital rectal exam (DRE) can often feel an enlarged prostate or nodules that suggest prostate cancer.• A biopsy is the only way to definitively diagnose prostate cancer.• A prostate biopsy can be guided by an ultrasound, MRI, or a combination of the two.• Prostate cancer is typically treated with surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, or a combination of these.

vignettes.response: Title: Advanced Prostate Cancer with Pelvic Lymphadenopathy and Pelvic Bone Metastases: A Case Report and Review of Advanced Prostate Cancer Diagnosis and Management.Abstract: This case report describes a 65-year-old man with advanced prostate cancer presenting with a three-month history of hip pain, difficulty walking, and urinary symptoms. The patient underwent a comprehensive physical examination, imaging studies, and laboratory tests, which confirmed a diagnosis of advanced prostate cancer with pelvic lymphadenopathy and pelvic bone metastases. The patient was treated with hormone therapy and chemotherapy, which resulted in partial remission of his symptoms. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of advanced prostate cancer to improve patient outcomes.Introduction: Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer among men in the United States, with over 191,930 new cases diagnosed in 2020. Advanced prostate cancer is defined as stage IV disease, which has metastasized beyond the prostate gland to other parts of the body. Symptoms of advanced prostate cancer can include urinary problems, pain, weight loss, and weakness. Diagnosis and treatment of advanced prostate cancer require a multidisciplinary approach involving medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, and other healthcare providers. This case report aims to highlight the diagnosis and management of advanced prostate cancer. Case Report: A 65-year-old man presented with a three-month history of hip pain, difficulty walking, and urinary symptoms. The patient had a past medical history of high blood pressure and hyperlipidemia. Physical examination revealed a firm, non-tender prostate gland, tenderness to palpation over the right hip, and decreased strength in both legs. Laboratory tests showed a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level of 81.9 ng/mL (normal range: 0-4 ng/mL) and an alkaline phosphatase level of 210 U/L (normal range: 38-126 U/L). Abdominal and pelvic computed tomography (CT) scans revealed multiple enlarged pelvic lymph nodes and a large soft tissue mass in the pelvis, which was suggestive of prostate cancer with pelvic lymphadenopathy and pelvic bone metastases (Figures 1-2). A bone scan showed numerous skeletal metastases, including the pelvis, spine, and skull. A transrectal ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy was performed, which revealed metastatic adenocarcinoma of the prostate. The patient was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer with pelvic lymphadenopathy and pelvic bone metastases. He was started on hormone therapy with leuprolide acetate and chemotherapy with docetaxel and prednisone. After four cycles of chemotherapy, the patient experienced a partial remission of his symptoms, with improved urinary function and decreased pelvic pain. He is currently undergoing regular follow-up with his oncologist.Discussion: This case report describes a patient with advanced prostate cancer presenting with symptoms of pelvic lymphadenopathy and pelvic bone metastases. The patient underwent a comprehensive physical examination, imaging studies, and laboratory tests, which confirmed a diagnosis of advanced prostate cancer. Treatment of advanced prostate cancer requires a multidisciplinary approach involving medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, and other healthcare providers. Hormone therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy are the primary treatment options for advanced prostate cancer. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of advanced prostate cancer to improve patient outcomes. Conclusion: Advanced prostate cancer is a serious condition that requires prompt diagnosis and treatment. This case report highlights the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to the diagnosis and management of advanced prostate cancer. Early diagnosis and treatment can improve patient outcomes and quality of life.

The patient reports having had no previous urinary complaints until the past week, when he developed a feeling of urinary urgency. Over the next few days, he noticed blood in his urine and developed frequent urination. He also reports intermittent pain in his lower back. The patient denies any recent fevers, cough, or other respiratory complaints. He also denies any changes in bowel habits, abdominal pain, or nausea. The patient denies any history of sexually transmitted infections. He denies any history of family members with prostate or other cancers. The patient reports that he is not taking any prescription medications and denies any over-the-counter or herbal supplement use. He reports drinking alcohol occasionally and quitting smoking 25 years ago.Physical exam:The patient is well-appearing and is in no acute distress. Vital signs are within normal limits: blood pressure 123/82 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, and respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute. On abdominal exam, the liver is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, but is nontender. On genitourinary exam, the bladder is full and tender on palpation. Urine culture is negative. PSA: 11.2 ng/mL. Prostate biopsy reveals a diagnosis of prostate adenocarcinoma. This case is unique because the patient is under the age of 50 and presents with acute urinary symptoms. These symptoms can be caused by prostatitis, urethral stricture, or prostate cancer. The most common treatment for prostate cancer is androgen deprivation therapy, which involves blocking the body's production of androgens or stopping the use of androgens altogether. Surgery and radiation are also effective treatment options. This case demonstrates the importance of a thorough history, physical exam, and laboratory testing in the diagnosis of prostate cancer, even in patients under the age of 50 with atypical symptoms.

She was diagnosed with SLE at the age of 16 years after presenting with arthritis and was found to have positive ANA, anti-dsDNA, and anti-Smith antibodies. She also had a renal biopsy that showed Lupus nephritis and proteinuria. Patient A was started on hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. The appendix was found to be inflamed and ruptured, and a perforation was found approximately 20 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve. The patient underwent an ileocecal resection with anastomosis. The patient's postoperative course was unremarkable, and she was discharged home after a few days. vignettes.prompt: Create a problem representation for a typical patient presenting with Lupus, including complete demographic characterization and relevant past medical history
vignettes.response: Lupus is a chronic autoimmune condition that can affect multiple organ systems. The condition is characterized by the production of autoantibodies against self-antigens. The cause of lupus is unknown, but it is thought to be related to a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Symptoms of lupus can include joint pain and swelling, skin rashes, fatigue, fever, and other symptoms. The most common form of the condition is systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), which can affect the skin, joints, kidneys, lungs, heart, and brain. Other forms of the condition include discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE), which affects the skin only, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE), which affects the skin and mucous membranes.

Lupus, or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease that can affect nearly any organ system in the body. It is more common in women than men, with a female to male ratio of about 9:1, and usually strikes between the ages of 15 and 44 . The disease can cause widespread inflammation and damage to tissues and organs, including the skin, joints, blood cells, kidneys, heart, and lungs. Lupus is caused by a combination of genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors. The genetic risk for lupus is thought to be about 30%, with several genetic variants having been linked to the disease. The most common environmental risk factor is sunlight exposure, which can trigger an immune response and lead to the production of autoantibodies. Hormonal factors, such as changes in estrogen levels during pregnancy, may also play a role in triggering lupus flares .

vignettes.response: Lupus is an autoimmune disease that can affect almost any part of the body. The disease can be characterized by a broad range of symptoms, including fatigue, joint pain, skin rashes, and swelling of the face. The disease can also cause damage to organs such as the kidneys, lungs, heart, and brain. It is estimated that 1.5 million Americans have lupus, and approximately 165,000 new cases are diagnosed each year. Lupus is more common in women, with 90% of cases affecting women between the ages of 15 and 44. However, it can also affect men and children. The cause of lupus is unknown, but it is believed to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Genetic factors may make a person more susceptible to developing the disease, while environmental factors such as sunlight exposure, infections, and certain medications may trigger the onset of symptoms. Lupus is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the production of autoantibodies that target self-cells and tissues. Lupus can affect multiple organs, including the skin, joints, kidneys, lungs, heart, and brain. The most common symptoms of lupus are fatigue, joint pain, and skin rashes. Other symptoms include fever, weight loss, anemia, and mouth ulcers. Diagnosing lupus can be challenging, as there is no one test that can confirm the disease. Instead, doctors will typically use a combination of blood tests, urine tests, and imaging studies to look for signs of organ damage. Treatment for lupus typically involves managing symptoms and reducing flares. This can involve a combination of medications, including anti-inflammatory drugs, antimalarial drugs, and corticosteroids. In severe cases, doctors may also recommend low-dose chemotherapy or other immunosuppressants.

vignettes.response: Title: Lupus Erythematosus Case Report 1: Clinical Presentation and Diagnostic Workup Objective: To identify the key manifestations of Lupus Erythematosus (LE) in a patient with a history of arthritis and pleural effusion and to conduct a diagnostic workup for LE. Background: Lupus Erythematosus (LE) is an autoimmune disease characterized by widespread inflammation of the connective tissues. The disease is most common in women and usually manifests in the third or fourth decade of life. It is a systemic disease that can affect the skin, joints, kidneys, lungs, and brain. It is diagnosed based on a combination of clinical findings and laboratory tests. The disease is treated with a combination of antimalarial drugs, steroids, and other immunosuppressive agents. Case Presentation: A 29-year-old female was brought to the emergency room with a chief complaint of pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. She had been experiencing these symptoms for the past 3 weeks. The patient stated that the pain was sharp and stabbing in nature and was worse with inspiration and lying flat. She also complained of a mild cough and intermittent fevers. She denied any prior history of rashes, photosensitivity, alopecia, or oral ulcers. Her past medical history was significant for arthritis, which was diagnosed 7 years ago and was treated with hydroxychloroquine. On physical exam, the patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. She had decreased breath sounds at the left lung base. Chest radiograph demonstrated a left lung opacity that was initially thought to represent a pleural effusion. The patient was taken to the operating room for a diagnostic thoracentesis, which revealed a turbid fluid with a white blood cell count of 3000 cells/mm3, a lymphocyte count of 92%, a protein level of 1.6 g/dL, and a glucose level of 15 mg/dL. She was started on ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and azithromycin. A CT scan of the chest revealed a left-sided pleural effusion, as well as swollen bilateral axillary lymph nodes and pericardial effusion. A CT scan of the abdomen showed no evidence of hepatosplenomegaly or renal involvement. The patient's arthritis was reevaluated, and a rheumatologist was consulted. The patient was diagnosed with LE based on a positive ANA, positive anti-dsDNA antibodies, and a positive antiphospholipid antibody panel. The patient was started on hydroxychloroquine, prednisone, and mycophenolate mofetil. Conclusion: Lupus Erythematosus is a complex autoimmune disease that can present with a wide range of symptoms. In this case, the patient presented with pleuritic chest pain and was diagnosed with a pleural effusion. Further diagnostic workup led to the diagnosis of LE. This case highlights the importance of a thorough history and physical exam, as well as the role of a multidisciplinary team in the diagnosis and management of complex diseases.

vignettes.prompt: Compose a brief presentation of a patient presenting with Tricuspid Endocarditis. Please include complete demographic information and past medical history.
vignettes.response: Tricuspid endocarditis (TE) is a rare condition that can lead to severe heart failure, cardiac arrest, and even death. The most common presenting symptoms of TE are new-onset heart failure, right-sided heart failure, and embolic events. The most common presenting symptoms of TE are new-onset heart failure, right-sided heart failure, and embolic events. It is most commonly caused by infection of the tricuspid valve by bacteria, but it can also be caused by fungi, parasites, or non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE). The most common organism responsible for TE is Staphylococcus aureus, followed by Streptococcus species. TE is often seen in patients with underlying conditions such as congenital heart disease, prior valvular surgery, intravenous drug use, prosthetic valves, and immunosuppression. Patients with TE may have a normal echocardiogram or show vegetations on the tricuspid valve, along with abnormal tricuspid valve motion, regurgitation, and/or annular calcification. The most common complications of TE are heart failure, valvular dysfunction, and embolic events. Diagnosis of TE requires a combination of clinical suspicion, echocardiography, and blood cultures. Treatment includes antimicrobial therapy and, in some cases, surgical intervention.

Objective: To present the case of a 76-year-old male patient who developed tricuspid endocarditis after undergoing multiple surgical procedures and was hospitalized for pneumonia. The patient's complex medical history and the management of his tricuspid endocarditis will be discussed.

A 76-year-old male patient with a history of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, aortic valve replacement surgery, carotid artery stenting, hypertension, and type II diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency room with dyspnea, cough, and fever. The patient had undergone CABG surgery six years prior and aortic valve replacement surgery two years prior. His post-surgical course had been complicated by a thrombus in the aorta, which required anticoagulation therapy for six months. The patient had a history of diabetes for 20 years and had been treated with oral hypoglycemic medications, including metformin and glibenclamide. The patient had a history of hypertension for 10 years and had been treated with beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. The patient was also taking clopidogrel to prevent thrombosis after the carotid artery stenting procedure.

Title: Tricuspid Endocarditis: A Case Report

Objective: To describe a case of tricuspid endocarditis in a patient with a history of rheumatic fever and to highlight the importance of prompt diagnosis and management of this condition.
 A 40-year-old female presented to the emergency room with a 3-day history of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. She had a past medical history of hypertension, rheumatic fever, and mitral valve replacement for stenosis 15 years earlier. She had no history of previous endocarditis, and she was not taking any medications at the time of presentation. She had no history of intravenous drug use, prosthetic valve, or implanted device. Physical examination revealed an afebrile, tachycardic female in moderate distress. On auscultation, there was a grade 2/6 systolic murmur over the mitral valve. She had a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 90% on room air, and a blood pressure of 160/80 mmHg. Initial laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 11.2 × 109/L, hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, and platelet count of 240 × 109/L. Her creatinine level was 1.1 mg/dL, and her troponin level was 0.03 ng/mL. Blood cultures were drawn, and the patient was started on intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for monitoring and was started on supplemental oxygen. She was noted to have a fever of 38.9°C. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed a normal left ventricular size and function, mild mitral regurgitation, and severe tricuspid regurgitation. There was also a 1.1 cm mass attached to the tricuspid valve leaflet (Figure 1). The mass was deemed to be a vegetation, and the patient was started on intravenous ampicillin. A transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) revealed a mass measuring 0.9 × 0.6 cm attached to the tricuspid valve (Figure 2). The mass was confirmed to be a vegetation, and the patient underwent open-heart surgery for mass removal. The patient had an uneventful postoperative course and was discharged home on postoperative day 5 on 6 weeks of amoxicillin-clavulanate. She was referred to the infectious disease clinic for follow-up. The vegetation was sent for culture, and it was positive for Staphylococcus aureus. The patient was referred for cardiology follow-up and was started on lifelong anticoagulation. She is currently doing well, with no signs or symptoms of recurrence of endocarditis.

Title: Tricuspid Endocarditis: A Case Report

Good morning, everyone. Today, I would like to present a case of a 53-year-old male who was admitted to the hospital with a fever and shortness of breath. The patient had a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and a recent diagnosis of prostate cancer. He had also undergone a radical prostatectomy about one year prior to the presentation. He had no history of drug use or prior surgical history. Upon admission, the patient was found to have a fever of 101.4 F, tachycardia with a heart rate of 110, and a blood pressure of 136/84 mmHg. Physical exam revealed an irregular heartbeat with a grade II/VI murmur heard at the left lower sternal border. Laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 12.9 K/cumm, a hemoglobin of 14.5 g/dL, and a platelet count of 312 K/cumm. Electrocardiogram showed a sinus tachycardia with an inverted T wave in lead III. Chest X-ray showed bilateral lung infiltrates. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed severe tricuspid regurgitation, a large mass on the tricuspid valve measuring about 3.1 cm by 1.5 cm (Figure 1), and a grade III diastolic deceleration. A transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) confirmed the diagnosis of tricuspid valve vegetation and showed additional vegetations on the aortic valve (Figure 2). The patient was started on antibiotics and was taken to the operating room for a tricuspid valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. The patient’s surgery went well and was discharged home four days later in stable condition. He was continued on antibiotics for a total of six weeks. At his three-month follow-up, the patient reported feeling well, and TEE showed a normal tricuspid valve with no evidence of recurrent vegetations.

Title: A Case of Tricuspid Endocarditis in an Elderly Female Patient 

Introduction: Tricuspid endocarditis (TE) is a rare but serious condition that can be caused by a variety of factors, including bacterial infections, cancer, and drug abuse. It can lead to heart failure, arrhythmia, and other complications. Early detection and treatment are important to prevent serious outcomes.

She had a grade III/VI systolic murmur over the tricuspid area. A transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) confirmed the presence of the mass and vegetation, as well as severe tricuspid regurgitation. Blood cultures grew streptococcus agalactiae, and antibiotics were initiated. She underwent emergent cardiac surgery, where the tricuspid valve was replaced with a mechanical valve and the vegetation was removed. Pathology of the valve and vegetation revealed gram-positive cocci, consistent with streptococcus agalactiae.

vignettes.response: Tricuspid endocarditis is a rare but potentially life-threatening condition that can occur in both native and prosthetic tricuspid valves. It is characterized by the presence of a vegetation on the tricuspid valve and can lead to valve dysfunction, heart failure, and other complications. The most common causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus, followed by viridans streptococci. Patients may present with a variety of symptoms, including fever, fatigue, dyspnea, cough, and chest pain. Diagnosis is typically made through the combination of echocardiography and blood cultures. Treatment usually involves a combination of antibiotics and surgery to remove the vegetation and repair or replace the valve.

vignettes.response: Tricuspid endocarditis (TE) is a serious condition that occurs when bacteria or other microorganisms infect the tricuspid valve of the heart. If the valve is damaged, it can allow blood to flow back into the lungs, which can cause serious complications such as heart failure and stroke. TE can be caused by a variety of factors, including bacterial infections, certain medical procedures, and genetic conditions. It is a serious condition that requires immediate medical attention.

Treatment typically involves a combination of antibiotics and surgery to replace the damaged valve.

vignettes.response: Tricuspid endocarditis (TE) is a rare but potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when a bacterial infection of the heart leads to inflammation and damage of the tricuspid valve. It is estimated to occur in less than 1% of all cases of endocarditis, with an incidence of approximately 0.1 cases per 100,000 person-years . The incidence of TE is much higher in patients with a congenital heart defect, with estimates ranging from 0.8% to 3.5% in these patients .

vignettes.response: Tricuspid endocarditis (TE) is a rare form of endocarditis that occurs in only 0.4-2% of all cases of endocarditis . It is more common in patients who have had a previous valve replacement, but it can also occur in patients with native tricuspid valves. The most common causative organism for TE is Staphylococcus aureus, followed by Streptococcus spp. and other Gram-negative bacilli . Patients with TE typically present with signs and symptoms of endocarditis, such as fever, heart murmur, and embolic phenomena. They may also present with signs of right-sided heart failure, such as peripheral edema, ascites, and hepatomegaly . Diagnosis of TE is made using a combination of echocardiography, blood cultures, and microbiological culture from valve tissue . Treatment of TE typically involves a combination of antibiotics and surgery to replace the valve .

Laboratory results showed white blood cell count of 11.64 × 109/L (4.0-10.0 × 109/L), hemoglobin of 12.4 g/dL (12.0-15.0 g/dL), platelet count of 145 × 109/L (140-340 × 109/L), and procalcitonin of 16.32 ng/mL (<0.05 ng/mL). vignettes.response: Title: Tricuspid Endocarditis in an HIV Patient with a Prosthetic Heart ValveCase Presentation:A 65-year-old male with a history of prosthetic tricuspid valve replacement 10 years ago and HIV presented to the clinic with complaints of orthopnea, increased shortness of breath, and lower extremity swelling. The patient was diagnosed with HIV 2 years ago and started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) consisting of emtricitabine, tenofovir, and efavirenz. The patient’s CD4+ cell count was 385 cells/mm3, and his viral load was undetectable. He also had a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type II diabetes. The patient reported that he had been non-compliant with his anticoagulation medication (warfarin) for the past month and had a warfarin level of 13.8. He denied any prior history of endocarditis, stroke, or deep vein thrombosis. On physical examination, he had a systolic murmur heard best at the tricuspid area. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema, and echocardiogram showed vegetations on the tricuspid valve (Figure 1). The patient was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation and treatment. His blood cultures and urine culture were positive for Staphylococcus aureus, and the patient underwent tricuspid valve replacement surgery. Discussion:This case is an important reminder of the increased risk of endocarditis in patients with prosthetic valves. The prevalence of endocarditis in these patients is 0.5% to 0.9% per patient-year.  The most common pathogen causing endocarditis in patients with prosthetic valves is viridans group streptococci, followed by Staphylococcus aureus. Patients with prosthetic valves are also at increased risk for endocarditis caused by Candida and Aspergillus species.  The presence of prosthetic valves also increases the risk of complications from endocarditis, such as valve destruction, valve dehiscence, and abscess formation.  Patients with prosthetic valves are also at increased risk for complications from anticoagulation therapy, such as bleeding and thrombosis. The optimal anticoagulation strategy for patients with prosthetic valves has not been established. However, the current guidelines recommend using vitamin K antagonists for mechanical valves and direct oral anticoagulants for mechanical valves with a high risk of thrombosis.  Patients with HIV are at increased risk for endocarditis due to the immunocompromised state caused by HIV and the use of HAART. The prevalence of endocarditis in patients with HIV is 3.9 to 5.6 per 1000 person-years.  The most common pathogens causing endocarditis in patients with HIV are Staphylococcus aureus and viridans group streptococci.  Patients with HIV are also at increased risk for complications from endocarditis, such as valve destruction, valve dehiscence, and abscess formation.  The optimal anticoagulation strategy for patients with HIV and prosthetic valves has not been established. However, the current guidelines recommend using vitamin K antagonists for mechanical valves and direct oral anticoagulants for mechanical valves with a high risk of thrombosis.  Conclusion:This case highlights the importance of considering endocarditis in patients with prosthetic valves and HIV. Patients with prosthetic valves are at increased risk for endocarditis, and the presence of HIV further increases this risk. It is important for medical providers to be aware of these risk factors and to have a low threshold for suspecting endocarditis in these patients. Early diagnosis and treatment of endocarditis in patients with prosthetic valves and HIV is crucial to preventing complications and improving outcomes.

Title: Tricuspid Endocarditis in a Patient with a Mechanical Heart Valve

Patient Information: Mr. J.P., a 64-year-old male with a history of severe heart failure, coronary artery disease, and a mechanical aortic valve replacement presented to the emergency room with a three-day history of worsening shortness of breath and a new onset of orthopnea. The patient reported a new onset of chest pain with exertion, but denied fever, chills, cough, or abdominal pain. His current medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, carvedilol, furosemide, lisinopril, warfarin, and digoxin. The patient’s past medical history was significant for hypertension, dyslipidemia, type II diabetes mellitus, and a previous myocardial infarction with a three-vessel bypass graft five years prior. The patient’s social history was significant for a 20-year smoking history and occasional alcohol use. The patient had no history of illicit drug use, recent travel, or family history of heart disease or endocarditis. Physical examination revealed an irregularly irregular heart rhythm with a rapid ventricular rate of 115 bpm. Auscultation of the heart revealed a loud systolic murmur heard at the apex and radiation to the axilla. Auscultation of the lungs revealed bibasilar crackles. The patient had no palpable lymphadenopathy, and the extremities revealed 1+ edema. The patient’s initial electrocardiogram revealed a wide-complex tachycardia with a leftward axis deviation, and the patient’s chest X-ray revealed bibasilar infiltrates (Figure 1). Laboratory findings included a white blood cell count of 10.9 K/uL, hemoglobin of 13.1 g/dL, platelet count of 170 K/uL, BNP of 250 pg/mL, D-dimer of 0.36 mg/L, and a normal troponin. The patient’s international normalized ratio (INR) was found to be 1.3, which was in the therapeutic range for his mechanical valve. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a severely dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 20% and severe hypokinesis of the anterior and anteroseptal walls. A large mass was seen on the anterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve measuring 1.6 cm × 2.3 cm, which was confirmed on transesophageal echocardiography (Figure 2). The patient was diagnosed with tricuspid valve endocarditis and was started on ampicillin/sulbactam and vancomycin. The patient was taken to the catheterization lab, and a left heart catheterization demonstrated mildly dilated coronary arteries with no significant stenosis. The patient was ultimately admitted to the intensive care unit and underwent successful open-heart surgery with the removal of the tricuspid valve vegetation and placement of a bioprosthetic tricuspid valve. The patient’s final pathology revealed a 1.8 cm × 2.4 cm vegetation on the anterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve, which was confirmed to be a fungal endocarditis caused by Aspergillus fumigatus. The patient’s postoperative course was complicated by sinus bradycardia requiring a permanent pacemaker and a recurrence of tricuspid valve endocarditis with the growth of Streptococcus mutans. The patient was ultimately discharged to a skilled nursing facility with plans for repeat surgery and lifelong anticoagulation therapy.
