Her medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). She was an ex-smoker and had quit smoking 10 years ago. vignettes.response: Title: A 70-year-old male with Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis presenting with right-sided heart failure and arrhythmia.Case Report:A 70-year-old male with a past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a prior stroke presented to the emergency department with a one-week history of palpitations and a one-day history of shortness of breath and orthopnea. He denied any cough, fever, or recent travel. His vitals on admission showed tachycardia with a heart rate of 150s, blood pressure of 120/60s, and oxygen saturation of 88%. His physical exam showed tachycardia with a grade III/VI systolic murmur in the tricuspid valve area. His chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema. His ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate. His CT angiogram of the chest showed no evidence of pulmonary embolism. His echocardiogram showed a grade III/VI systolic regurgitation in the tricuspid valve area with a large vegetation, severe right ventricular systolic dysfunction, and severe right atrial dilatation (Figures 1-2). Blood cultures were positive for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone and underwent a tricuspid valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. His hospital course was complicated by a large right pleural effusion that required drainage and an episode of atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate that required cardioversion. He was discharged on a four-week course of ceftriaxone and a lifelong regimen of oral anticoagulation.Discussion:Tricuspid valve endocarditis is uncommon, accounting for less than 1% of all cases of endocarditis. The most common cause of tricuspid valve endocarditis is bacterial endocarditis following surgery on the right side of the heart or the pulmonary circulation. Other causes include intravenous drug use, pacemaker leads, and indwelling catheters. The most common pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus, followed by Streptococcus spp. and Gram-negative bacilli. Clinical manifestations include fever, dyspnea, and signs of right-sided heart failure. Echocardiogram shows a vegetation on the tricuspid valve with regurgitation and possible valvular perforation. Blood cultures are positive in about 50% of cases. Diagnosis is made using the Duke criteria with the addition of a positive echocardiogram. Treatment involves a combination of antibiotics and surgical intervention if there is valvular destruction, perforation, or persistent bacteremia despite antibiotics. Antibiotic treatment is recommended for four to six weeks. Surgical intervention is recommended if there is valvular destruction, perforation, or persistent bacteremia despite antibiotics. Surgery involves valve replacement or valvular repair and debridement of the endocardium. Prognosis is poor, with a mortality rate of 20-40%.The teaching objective of this case is to teach medical students the clinical manifestations, diagnosis, and treatment of tricuspid valve endocarditis. The key teaching point is that tricuspid valve endocarditis is rare but should be considered in patients with right-sided heart failure, especially if there is a history of valvular disease, intravenous drug use, or indwelling catheters. Echocardiogram is the diagnostic test of choice, and treatment involves a combination of antibiotics and surgical intervention if indicated.

Title: Tricuspid Endocarditis: A Case Report 

Case: A 42-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. He denied chest pain, palpitations, or weight loss. He had a past medical history of hypertension and a family history of atherosclerotic disease. On physical examination, he was afebrile and his vital signs were within normal limits. He was found to have a 3/6 systolic murmur at the right lower sternal border. Laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 10.6 × 103 cells/μL, hemoglobin of 12.2 g/dL, platelet count of 236 × 103 cells/μL, creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein of 187 mg/L. Chest radiography and electrocardiogram were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 4.6 × 5.1 cm mass attached to the anterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve with severe tricuspid regurgitation (Figure 1). The valve leaflets were thickened and immobile, and the right ventricle was moderately enlarged. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed the findings of transthoracic echocardiography and showed a second mass attached to the posterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve (Figure 2). Blood cultures were collected and empiric treatment with vancomycin and ceftriaxone was initiated. The patient was prepared for emergent tricuspid valve replacement. During the surgery, the valve was found to be heavily calcified and the tricuspid annulus was dilated. The valve leaflets were fused and were not able to be separated. The valve was replaced with a 31 mm St. Jude Medical Epic stented pericardial valve. The postoperative course was uncomplicated, and the patient was discharged from the hospital on postoperative day 10. Blood cultures returned negative, and the patient was started on amoxicillin and clavulanate for 6 weeks.

The duration of antibiotic therapy for tricuspid valve endocarditis is typically 4-6 weeks.

She denies any recent travel or exposure to sick contacts. She has a past medical history of hypertension, diabetes, and asthma but no history of rheumatic heart disease. Her physical exam is notable for tachycardia, tachypnea, and oxygen saturation of 90%. Her lungs are clear on auscultation, and she has no murmurs or gallops on cardiac exam. Chest x-ray reveals diffuse interstitial infiltrates. Blood tests show leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers. Computed tomography of the chest reveals bilateral infiltrates. She is started on antibiotics and admitted to the hospital. Further workup is notable for positive blood cultures for Streptococcus gallolyticus and a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealing vegetation on the tricuspid valve. The patient is diagnosed with tricuspid endocarditis and is started on appropriate antibiotics. She undergoes a surgical valve replacement and recovers well.Discussion: Tricuspid endocarditis is a rare form of endocarditis that accounts for approximately 2-3% of all cases. It is most commonly caused by Streptococcus species, followed by Staphylococcus species. Patients may present with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and weight loss. They may also have signs of endocarditis, such as a new heart murmur, splenomegaly, and embolic phenomena. The most common complication of tricuspid endocarditis is systemic embolization, which can affect the brain, kidneys, spleen, and other organs. Diagnosis is made through a combination of blood cultures, TTE, and transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE). Treatment involves antibiotics and, in some cases, surgical valve replacement. The prognosis of tricuspid endocarditis depends on the causative organism and the presence of complications.

Case Presentation: 
 Mrs. R. is a 61-year-old African American woman, with a past medical history significant for hypertension, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and chronic kidney disease. She is a life-time non-smoker and denies any history of alcohol or illicit drug use. She is married with four children and works as a registered nurse in an outpatient clinic. She underwent a CT of the abdomen and pelvis, which revealed a 2.9 cm mass in the ascending colon with no evidence of metastatic disease. A positron emission tomography (PET) scan demonstrated increased FDG uptake in the ascending colon with no evidence of distant metastatic disease. She was diagnosed with a Stage III, well-differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon.

Title: Colon Cancer: A Case Report for Medical Students

Case: A 55-year-old woman presented to the clinic with a 1-month history of diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and pain in her left lower abdomen. She also complained of a 20-pound weight loss and fatigue over the same period. Her past medical history was significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a family history of colon cancer. A colonoscopy revealed a 1.5 cm polypoid lesion in the sigmoid colon, which was removed using endoscopic mucosal resection. The histopathological examination revealed a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, and lymph node metastasis. Immunohistochemical staining revealed positive staining for CK20, CDX2, and BAP1 and negative staining for CK7 and MLH1. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple bilateral lung metastases, multiple liver metastases, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. The patient's diagnosis was stage IV colorectal cancer (CRC). She was started on palliative chemotherapy and is currently receiving second-line chemotherapy.

His peripheral pulse oximetry showed an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air, which improved to 93% on a nasal prong. His routine laboratory workup was normal except for C-reactive protein which was 10.9 mg/L (normal range 0-10 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate which was 52 mm/hour (normal range 0-15 mm/hour). His chest x-ray was suggestive of patchy infiltration in both lung fields (Figure 1). His sputum sample was sent for culture and sensitivity test, which came back positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Discussion: Bacterial pneumonia is an infection of the lower respiratory tract that is commonly caused by bacteria, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. In the elderly population, the most common cause of bacterial pneumonia is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram-positive bacterium that is spread through the air via respiratory droplets. It can cause an acute infection that affects the mucous membranes of the sinuses, throat, and lungs. Symptoms of bacterial pneumonia include cough, productive sputum, shortness of breath, fever, and chest pain. Diagnosis is made through a combination of history, physical exam, and laboratory tests. Chest x-ray can reveal areas of consolidation, and blood cultures can confirm the diagnosis. Treatment of bacterial pneumonia involves the use of antibiotics, which can be given intravenously or orally depending on the severity of the infection. Intravenous antibiotics are typically used in cases of severe pneumonia, while oral antibiotics can be used in cases of mild or moderate pneumonia. Antibiotics are usually given for 5 to 7 days, but the length of treatment may vary depending on the patient's response to therapy. In this case, the patient was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and oral prednisone.

He denies any recent travel, sick contacts, or hospital visits.Past Medical History: The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia. The patient states that he is allergic to penicillin but is not allergic to any other medications.Physical Examination: The patient is in moderate distress. His vital signs are: temperature of 101 degrees Fahrenheit, heart rate of 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure of 142/90 millimeters of mercury, and oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. The patient has coarse breath sounds and crackles on lung examination. The patient's abdomen is soft and nondistended with normoactive bowel sounds. The patient's extremities are warm and well perfused.Laboratory Findings: The patient's initial laboratory findings include a white blood cell count of 13.2 thousand cells per microliter with 90% neutrophils, a hemoglobin level of 14.3 grams per deciliter, a platelet count of 211 thousand cells per microliter, a sodium level of 137 millimoles per liter, a potassium level of 4.2 millimoles per liter, a chloride level of 99 millimoles per liter, a carbon dioxide level of 24 millimoles per liter, a blood urea nitrogen level of 20 milligrams per deciliter, a creatinine level of 1.09 milligrams per deciliter, and a glucose level of 150 milligrams per deciliter. vignettes.response: Bacterial pneumonia is a common infection of the lower respiratory tract that causes inflammation and infection of the lungs. It is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, particularly in developing countries, and is a major cause of childhood death. Pneumonia can be caused by a variety of pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi. Bacterial pneumonia is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, a Gram-positive bacterium that is also known as pneumococcus. Other common causes of bacterial pneumonia include Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella pneumophila, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. In recent years, the incidence of pneumonia has increased due to antibiotic resistance and an aging population. It is important for medical students to be able to diagnose and treat pneumonia effectively.

Laboratory studies revealed a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) at a titer of 1:1280, positive anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (anti-CCP) at a titer of 101 U/mL (normal < 20 U/mL), and rheumatoid factor (RF) of 35 U/mL (normal < 14 U/mL). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 70 mm/h, and C-reactive protein (CRP) was 11.4 mg/dL. IgM osteopontin (OPN) was elevated at 19.6 ng/mL (normal range: 0-10 ng/mL). HLA-B27 was negative. Radiographs of the bilateral hand and wrist demonstrated erosive changes involving the second carpometacarpal (CMC) joint, with mild erosion of the third CMC joint and no erosions of the wrist joints (Figures 3-4). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the right hand revealed synovitis and tenosynovitis of the second and third PIP joints, as well as erosive changes in the second CMC joint (Figure 5). The patient was diagnosed with RA based on her clinical presentation and laboratory findings. She was started on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily and prednisone 40 mg daily. The patient’s pain and swelling improved over time, and her inflammatory markers normalized. She was referred to the rheumatology clinic for follow-up and continued on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily and prednisone 40 mg daily. She was seen again in the clinic two months later with a significant improvement in her symptoms and inflammatory markers. She was started on methotrexate 25 mg weekly and tapered off of the prednisone. The patient was seen again four months later and was doing well with no joint pain or swelling. She continued on methotrexate 25 mg weekly and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily.

vignettes.response: Title: Rheumatoid Arthritis Case Report 1. Introduction: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic, inflammatory, autoimmune disease that affects the joints and can be associated with extra-articular manifestations. It typically affects middle-aged women. RA is characterized by synovial inflammation and hyperplasia, resulting in erosion and damage of cartilage and bone, leading to deformity, disability, and joint stiffness. 2. Case Report: A 45-year-old female with no significant past medical history presents with a two-week history of pain in her fingers, wrist, and knees. The pain is constant and worsens with activity, making it difficult for her to perform her daily activities. The patient reports that she has had similar symptoms in the past, which lasted for a few days and then resolved on their own. However, this time the pain has persisted for two weeks and is getting worse. She denies any recent trauma, fever, chills, or other symptoms. On physical examination, the patient is in moderate distress due to the pain. Her hands are swollen and stiff, especially in the mornings. Her knees are also swollen and tender to palpation. No other joints are affected. Laboratory tests are significant for an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 80 mm/h (normal: 0–20 mm/h) and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 10 mg/dL (normal: < 0.6 mg/dL). X-rays of the hands and knees are unremarkable. Based on the patient's symptoms and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of RA is made. 3. Discussion: RA is a chronic, autoimmune, inflammatory disease that affects the joints and can cause significant disability if not treated properly. The exact cause of RA is unknown, but it is thought to be related to a combination of genetic, environmental, and immune factors. The disease affects women more than men, with a ratio of 3:1. RA typically affects middle-aged adults, but it can affect people of all ages. The symptoms of RA can include joint pain, swelling, and stiffness; fatigue; and low-grade fever. The most common joints affected are the small joints in the hands and wrists, but any joint can be affected. The diagnosis of RA is based on a combination of factors, including symptoms, physical examination, laboratory tests, and imaging studies. The treatment of RA typically involves a combination of medications, including disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and corticosteroids. Early diagnosis and treatment of RA are important to prevent joint damage and disability.

vignettes.response: Case Title: Rheumatoid Arthritis Case Title: A 50-year-old woman with a 10-year history of RA presented with worsening joint pain and stiffness. Case Description: A 50-year-old woman presented to the clinic with a 10-year history of RA. She complained of worsening joint pain and stiffness in her hands, feet, knees, and elbows. She had been diagnosed with RA 10 years ago and was initially treated with methotrexate and prednisone. After two years, she was switched to adalimumab, an anti-TNF agent, due to inadequate response to the previous treatment. Despite adalimumab treatment, she continued to experience pain and swelling in her joints, especially in her hands, feet, knees, and elbows. She denied any morning stiffness, fatigue, or other symptoms. She had no history of other autoimmune diseases. On physical examination, she had swelling and tenderness in her hands, feet, knees, and elbows. Her joints were warm and tender to palpation. She had limited range of motion in her small joints of her hands and feet. She had no palmar or pulmonary edema. Laboratory testing was notable for a CRP of 2.8 mg/dL (normal < 0.5 mg/dL) and ESR of 110 mm/hr. (normal < 20 mm/hr.). She also had normal kidney function and liver enzymes. X-rays of her hands and feet showed erosive changes in her joints, but there was no evidence of bone destruction or joint space narrowing. She was diagnosed with RA and was started on adalimumab. After six months of treatment, she had mild improvement in her symptoms, but she continued to have pain and swelling in her hands, feet, knees, and elbows. She was switched to tocilizumab, an anti-IL-6 agent, due to inadequate response to adalimumab. After one month of tocilizumab treatment, she had significant improvement in her symptoms, including reduced pain and stiffness in her joints, and increased range of motion in her small joints. She was able to perform her daily activities with minimal difficulty. She continued to do well on tocilizumab and had no further flares or complications. Case Discussion: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, autoimmune, inflammatory disease characterized by synovial inflammation and progressive joint destruction. It affects approximately 0.5 to 1% of the general population and is more common in women than in men. The etiology of RA is unknown, but it is believed to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Patients with RA typically present with morning stiffness, joint pain, swelling, and tenderness. They may also have fatigue and low-grade fever. Over time, untreated RA can lead to joint damage and deformity, which can significantly impact function and quality of life. The current mainstay of RA treatment is a combination of conventional synthetic (cs) and biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). csDMARDs include methotrexate, leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine, and sulfasalazine. bDMARDs include anti-TNF agents (adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab), anti-IL-6 agents (tocilizumab), anti-IL-17 agents (secukinumab, ixekizumab), and anti-CD20 agents (rituximab). Patients who do not respond to csDMARDs are typically started on bDMARDs. Patients who fail to respond to bDMARDs may be switched to a different bDMARD or have their current bDMARD combined with a csDMARD. The choice of csDMARD is often based on the patient's comorbidities and risk of adverse events. Patients with RA should be evaluated for other autoimmune diseases, as they often co-exist with RA. Early diagnosis and treatment of RA are important to prevent joint damage and improve function and quality of life.

Title: Multiple Sclerosis: A Comprehensive Overview of a Complex Disease. 
 Introduction: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, inflammatory, and degenerative disease of the central nervous system (CNS), affecting over 2.3 million people worldwide . The disease is characterized by a wide range of symptoms, including muscle weakness, fatigue, vision loss, cognitive impairment, and difficulty walking. The presentation of MS can vary greatly depending on the affected regions of the CNS.  The exact cause of MS remains unknown, but it is believed to be an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks myelin sheaths, the fatty covering of nerve cells.  Demographics: MS is most commonly diagnosed in people aged 20–40 and affects women at a higher rate than men.  While the exact cause of MS is unknown, genetic and environmental factors are thought to play a role.  MS can be divided into two main types: relapsing-remitting and primary progressive.  The relapsing-remitting form of MS accounts for 85% of cases and is characterized by periods of symptomatic attacks followed by periods of remission.  The primary progressive form of MS accounts for the remaining 15% of cases and is characterized by a gradual worsening of symptoms without remission periods.  Past Medical History: The patient, a 35-year-old female, presented to our clinic with a 5-year history of numbness in her left hand, which progressed to her right hand and feet. She also reported difficulty walking and had recently fallen several times. She had a history of migraines, but no other significant past medical history. Physical Examination: On physical examination, the patient had normal vital signs and a normal neurological examination. She had normal cranial nerves, normal muscle strength in her extremities, and no sensory deficits. MRI of the brain showed multiple lesions, some with contrast enhancement, consistent with demyelination.  Conclusion: Based on the patient's symptoms and medical history, as well as the results of her neurological examination and MRI, she was diagnosed with relapsing-remitting MS.  The patient was started on a course of steroids to reduce inflammation and was referred to a neurologist for further management.

Laboratory results were significant for white blood cell count of 4.9 × 109/L, hemoglobin of 13.8 g/dL, platelets of 228 × 109/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/h. An autoimmune workup was negative. The patient's LFTs were significantly elevated, and she was referred for a liver biopsy. The biopsy showed no significant fibrosis, and there was no evidence of autoimmune hepatitis. However, it was noted that the portal tracts contained lymphocytes, which were positive for CD20, CD3, and CD8. Immunohistochemistry showed that the infiltrating cells were positive for aquaporin 4 (AQP4). The biopsy findings were consistent with autoimmune hepatitis associated with MS. The patient was started on steroids and had a significant improvement in her LFTs.

vignettes.response: Problem Representation: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, progressive, inflammatory autoimmune disease of the central nervous system. The disease is characterized by focal demyelination, loss of myelin-producing oligodendrocytes, and axonal damage. The pathogenesis of MS involves the migration of autoreactive T-cells across the blood–brain barrier, which leads to the activation of macrophages and the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, ultimately resulting in demyelination and axonal damage . The clinical presentation of MS is heterogeneous, ranging from a clinically isolated syndrome to progressive physical, sensory, cognitive, and psychiatric impairments.

vignettes.prompt: Create a problem representation for a typical patient presenting with Multiple Sclerosis, including complete demographic characterization and relevant past medical history
vignettes.response: Problem Representation: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system (CNS) affecting the myelin sheaths surrounding neurons. It is the most common autoimmune disease of the CNS, affecting over 2.1 million people globally, with the highest incidence in North America and Europe, and a lower incidence in Africa and Asia. MS is 2–3 times more common in women than men, with an average age of onset of approximately 30 years of age . The etiology of MS remains unknown, but it is thought to be a complex interplay between genetic, environmental, and immune factors. The clinical presentation of MS is heterogeneous, with a wide range of symptoms depending on the location of the lesions in the CNS. Common symptoms include optic neuritis, sensory disturbances, limb weakness, limb numbness, double vision, and dysarthria. Diagnosis of MS requires the presence of two or more clinically isolated demyelinating events, with evidence of dissemination in space and time .

vignettes.response: As an expert in the field of healthcare, I can provide you with a general overview of the problem representation for a patient presenting with Multiple Sclerosis (MS). MS is a chronic, inflammatory, and demyelinating autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS) that affects the myelin sheath of neurons, leading to axonal degeneration and neuronal loss. It is the most common neurological disorder in young adults, affecting up to 2.5 million people worldwide. The pathogenesis of MS involves a complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors that result in the breakdown of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) and the infiltration of T lymphocytes into the CNS, where they initiate an inflammatory cascade that causes demyelination and axonal damage. The disease presentation is highly variable, with the most common symptoms including fatigue, cognitive impairment, pain, weakness, spasticity, and gait disturbances. Diagnosis of MS is based on the McDonald criteria, which include the presence of disseminated lesions in space and time, along with evidence of CNS inflammation. The most common diagnostic tool is magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which can detect the presence of lesions in the brain and spinal cord. There is no cure for MS, but the available disease-modifying therapies can help to slow the progression of the disease and manage symptoms. The prognosis of MS is highly variable, with some patients experiencing only mild symptoms, while others may experience severe disability.

She received treatment with the anti-viral medication, famciclovir, and underwent a pleural biopsy to confirm the diagnosis. Title: Management of Acute Exacerbation of Multiple Sclerosis with IV Methylprednisolone: A Case Report. 

Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, autoimmune, demyelinating, inflammatory, neurological disorder characterized by a wide range of symptoms and varying degrees of disability. This case report describes the management of an acute exacerbation of MS with IV methylprednisolone. The patient was a 35-year-old woman with a past medical history of MS, hypertension, and an unrelated history of transient ischemic attack (TIA). She presented to the emergency department with complaints of severe back pain, bilateral lower extremity weakness, and difficulty ambulating. Clinical examination revealed decreased lower extremity strength and a positive Babinski sign. MRI of the brain and spinal cord revealed multiple MS-like lesions in the brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord. The patient was diagnosed with an acute exacerbation of MS and was treated with a course of IV methylprednisolone. Over the course of treatment, her symptoms improved, and she was discharged home with a follow-up appointment with her neurologist. This case report highlights the importance of prompt diagnosis and treatment of acute exacerbations of MS with IV methylprednisolone to minimize long-term disability.

vignettes.response: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune neurological disorder that affects the central nervous system and results in demyelination of the nerve fibers. The disorder is more prevalent in women, with an estimated 2.3 times higher risk of developing the disease than men . The disease usually manifests itself between the ages of 20 and 40, and there is no known cure. The onset of the disease can be gradual or sudden, and symptoms vary from mild to severe. MS is a lifelong disease that can cause significant disability, especially in the later stages. The etiology of MS is still unknown, but it is believed to be an autoimmune response that attacks the myelin sheath surrounding the nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. The disease is characterized by periods of remission and relapse, and the course of the disease varies widely from person to person. The treatment of MS is focused on reducing the frequency and severity of relapses and managing symptoms. Treatment options include medications, physical therapy, and rehabilitation.

vignettes.response: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. The clinical presentation and course of MS are highly heterogeneous, and the disease is characterized by a wide range of neurological symptoms, including optic neuritis, cerebellar ataxia, motor weakness, sensory loss, urinary incontinence, and sexual dysfunction. The disease most commonly affects young adults, typically between the ages of 20 and 40, and is more common in women than men. The etiology of MS is not fully understood, but it is believed to involve both genetic and environmental factors. Several genetic factors have been identified as being associated with an increased risk of developing MS, including variants in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and other genes involved in immune regulation. Environmental factors such as smoking, vitamin D deficiency, and exposure to certain viral infections may also contribute to the development of MS. The diagnosis of MS is based on a combination of clinical symptoms, neurological examination, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spinal cord. MRI is used to detect lesions in the white matter of the brain and spinal cord, which are characteristic of MS. These lesions can be detected using T2-weighted MRI, which shows areas of increased signal intensity, and T1-weighted MRI, which shows areas of reduced signal intensity. The prognosis of MS is highly variable, and the disease course can range from relatively mild to severe. Treatment options for MS include medications to reduce inflammation, such as interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, and dimethyl fumarate, and medications to manage symptoms such as pain and spasticity.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a neurological disorder that affects the central nervous system (CNS) and is characterized by the demyelination of nerve fibers in the CNS. It is a common neurological disorder that affects more than 2 million people worldwide. MS typically affects young adults, with a peak incidence in the 20s and 30s. It is more common in women, with a female-to-male ratio of 2.5:1. The exact cause of MS is unknown, but it is thought to be an autoimmune disorder that occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks myelin, the fatty insulating sheath that covers nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. This results in damage to the myelin and a loss of nerve function. The symptoms of MS can vary widely, depending on the location of the damage in the CNS. Common symptoms include fatigue, weakness, numbness, balance problems, pain, sexual dysfunction, depression, and cognitive problems. The course of MS is unpredictable, with periods of remission and relapse. There is no cure for MS, but there are treatments that can help manage the symptoms and slow the progression of the disease.

vignettes.response: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that affects more than 2.8 million people worldwide. It is the most common neurological disease affecting young adults. The diagnosis of MS is complex and requires the use of several diagnostic tests, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and evoked potentials. However, the definitive diagnosis of MS can only be made by the presence of disseminated lesions in time and space, with a minimum of one lesion in each cerebral hemisphere, one in the spinal cord, and one in the optic nerve, or if there are lesions in at least two of these locations, excluding the optic nerve. The most common symptoms of MS include fatigue, vision problems, muscle weakness, and trouble with coordination and balance. Other symptoms can include pain, sexual dysfunction, and cognitive problems. The exact cause of MS is unknown, but it is believed to be an autoimmune disease in which the body's immune system attacks myelin, the insulating substance around nerve fibers. There is currently no cure for MS, but treatments can help manage symptoms and slow the progression of the disease.

Multiple myeloma is a type of cancer that affects the plasma cells in the bone marrow. It is characterized by the overproduction of a specific type of antibody, often resulting in elevated levels of antibodies in the blood. This can lead to a variety of complications, including anemia, bone loss, and kidney damage. Although multiple myeloma is a rare type of cancer, it is the second most common blood cancer after leukemia.Slide 3: Risk factors for multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma can occur at any age, but it is most commonly diagnosed in people over the age of 60. Men are more likely to develop multiple myeloma than women. The exact cause of multiple myeloma is unknown, but there are several risk factors that may increase the likelihood of developing the disease, including family history of multiple myeloma, certain genetic factors, exposure to certain chemicals or radiation, and chronic autoimmune conditions.Slide 4: Signs and symptoms of multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma can cause a variety of signs and symptoms, including fatigue, pain in the bones, infections, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, weight loss, and anemia. These signs and symptoms are often vague and may not be specific to multiple myeloma, so it is important for anyone experiencing these symptoms to see a healthcare provider to determine the underlying cause.Slide 5: Diagnosis of multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is often diagnosed using a combination of blood tests, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, and imaging studies such as X-rays, MRI, or PET scans. These tests are used to look for signs of multiple myeloma in the blood, bone marrow, and organs outside of the bone marrow.Slide 6: Treatment of multiple myeloma. The treatment of multiple myeloma typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and stem cell transplant. The specific treatment plan for each individual will depend on several factors, including the stage of the cancer, the age and overall health of the patient, and the presence of other health conditions.

vignettes.response: Multiple Myeloma (MM) is a malignant plasma cell disorder and the second most common hematological malignancy, accounting for about 1% of all cancers and 17% of all hematologic malignancies. The incidence of MM is increasing worldwide, and it is expected to increase further in the future due to the aging population. The median age at diagnosis is 69 years, and it is more common in men than in women. The incidence of MM is higher in industrialized countries, and it is the most common hematological malignancy in the United States. MM is characterized by monoclonal expansion of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow, leading to a variety of clinical manifestations, including bone pain, bone lesions, anemia, renal failure, hypercalcemia, and immunodeficiency. Diagnosis of MM is based on the presence of monoclonal plasma cells in the bone marrow and/or monoclonal protein in the blood or urine. Treatment options for MM include chemotherapy, autologous stem cell transplant, and targeted therapies. The prognosis of MM has improved significantly in recent years due to the use of novel targeted therapies.

Patient's LDH and beta-2 microglobulin were elevated. Patient's serum protein electrophoresis showed a monoclonal spike. Patient's cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was negative for pleocytosis, and protein electrophoresis showed a monoclonal spike. Patient's serum immunofixation electrophoresis showed an IgG lambda monoclonal spike. Patient's bone marrow biopsy showed a high percentage of plasma cells with lambda restriction and a high-risk cytogenetic profile. Patient's MRI of the spine showed a T2 hyperintensity in the cervical spinal cord. Patient was diagnosed with multiple myeloma with spinal cord compression. Patient was treated with radiation therapy and was started on dexamethasone. Patient was discharged home on a steroid taper and follow-up to outpatient oncology clinic.

vignettes.prompt: Create a problem representation for a typical patient presenting with Multiple Myeloma, including complete demographic characterization and relevant past medical history
vignettes.response: Problem Representation: Multiple Myeloma (MM) is a malignancy of plasma cells that resides primarily in the bone marrow (BM). The clinical features of MM are diverse and may include anemia, fatigue, back pain, hypercalcemia, osteoporotic fractures, infections, and peripheral neuropathy . Symptoms of MM typically present after the emergence of a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) or smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM) . Diagnosis of MM requires a bone marrow biopsy to demonstrate a clonal plasma cell infiltrate greater than 60% of the overall cellularity, with overt evidence of active plasma cell secretion of an immunoglobulin. MM is a heterogeneous disease with a wide range of clinical behavior, with some patients surviving for many years without treatment and others rapidly progressing and succumbing to the disease. The current standard of care for patients with newly diagnosed MM involves induction therapy with quadruplets of novel agents and steroids, followed by autologous stem cell transplant in fit patients . Maintenance therapy with novel agents is used for patients with standard-risk disease, whereas patients with high-risk disease may be treated with novel agent-based doublets or triplet therapy . Patients who are not transplanted upfront are treated with a triplet regimen consisting of a proteasome inhibitor, immunomodulatory agent, and steroids . At relapse, treatment options include novel agent-based doublets or triplets, autologous stem cell transplant, or monoclonal antibody-based regimens.

On physical examination, the patient had a palpable mass in the lower back. Laboratory findings included a white blood cell count of 4.39 x 10^9/L (reference range 3.5-11 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin of 12.6 g/dL (reference range 13.5-17.5 g/dL), and platelet count of 228 x 10^9/L (reference range 150-450 x 10^9/L). A serum free light chain assay showed an elevated kappa light chain level of 48,330 mg/L (reference range 3.3-26.3 mg/L) and an elevated lambda light chain level of 153 mg/L (reference range 5.7-26.3 mg/L), resulting in a kappa/lambda ratio of 319.5. A urine immunofixation assay showed no monoclonal protein. Bone marrow biopsy and aspiration were performed, which revealed a monoclonal plasma cell population consisting of 50% plasma cells, with cytogenetic analysis revealing a normal male karyotype. Flow cytometry was performed, which showed a monoclonal kappa restricted plasma cell population consisting of 12% plasma cells. The patient was diagnosed with IgG kappa MM and was started on bortezomib and dexamethasone. After one cycle of therapy, the patient had a significant improvement in his back pain and underwent a repeat bone marrow biopsy, which showed a decrease in the plasma cell infiltration to 15% with no monoclonal spike. The patient was started on lenalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone. After one cycle of this treatment regimen, the patient was noted to have persistent back pain, and a repeat bone marrow biopsy was performed, which revealed a 40% plasma cell infiltration. The patient was restarted on bortezomib and dexamethasone, and after one cycle of therapy, a repeat bone marrow biopsy showed a 20% plasma cell infiltration with no monoclonal spike. The patient is currently in complete remission with no evidence of disease by bone marrow biopsy, with a plan to proceed with an autologous stem cell transplant once the patient has had adequate treatment.

vignettes.response: Multiple myeloma is a type of cancer that develops in plasma cells. These cells are responsible for producing antibodies to fight infections. In multiple myeloma, these cells multiply in an out of control manner and accumulate in the bone marrow, leading to bone damage and other complications. It is a rare type of cancer, with an estimated 3100 new cases diagnosed each year in the United States. The average age of diagnosis is 69 years, and it is more common in men than women. The exact cause of multiple myeloma is unknown, but there are several risk factors that have been identified. These include advanced age, family history of the disease, certain genetic conditions, exposure to radiation, and certain environmental toxins. Treatment options for multiple myeloma include chemotherapy, stem cell transplant, radiation, and targeted therapies. The prognosis for multiple myeloma varies depending on the stage of the disease and the specific subtype. With appropriate treatment, some patients may be cured, while others may experience a prolonged remission.

The exact cause of MM is unknown, but it is thought to be related to exposure to certain environmental factors, such as radiation, chemical toxins, and certain viruses. MM can also be related to certain genetic factors, such as a family history of the disease. Treatment for MM typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, radiation, and stem cell transplantation. Despite these treatments, MM is a difficult to cure cancer, with a median survival of 3 to 6 years.

His past medical history was significant for hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3, and coronary artery disease. He had no history of smoking or illicit drug use. Physical examination revealed tenderness over the back. Laboratory workup was significant for hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL, albumin of 3.5 g/dL, calcium of 9.4 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 300 U/L, and beta-2 microglobulin of 11.9 mg/L. A bone marrow biopsy was performed and showed 75% kappa light chain restricted plasma cells. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis revealed the presence of t(4;14) translocation and del(17p). A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated diffuse osteosclerosis and multiple lytic lesions in the skull, vertebral bodies, ribs, and pelvis. A MRI of the spine demonstrated multiple T2 hyperintense lesions and compression of the spinal cord at the C3 and C4 vertebral levels. A CT scan of the skull showed a lytic lesion involving the posterior aspect of the frontal bone. A lumbar puncture was performed and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed an elevated protein level of 1,400 mg/dL and no pleocytosis. A repeat CBC showed a reduction in absolute monoclonal lymphocyte count to 72,200/mm3. A diagnosis of multiple myeloma was made and the patient was started on induction therapy with bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone. His symptoms improved, and follow-up MRI of the spine showed a decrease in the size of the spinal cord lesions.Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of considering multiple myeloma in the differential diagnosis of patients with back pain and fatigue, particularly in those with risk factors such as advanced age, chronic kidney disease, and monoclonal gammopathy. vignettes.response: Title: A 69-year-old male with multiple myeloma presents with a six-month history of progressive fatigue and bone pain.Case: A 69-year-old male presents to the outpatient clinic with a six-month history of progressive fatigue, weakness, and bone pain. He denies any constitutional symptoms. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia. He is on losartan, metformin, and atorvastatin. Family history is significant for multiple myeloma in the father. Physical examination is significant for tenderness on palpation of the lumbar spine, multiple tender subcutaneous nodules on the extremities, and pallor. Lab findings are significant for anemia (Hb 9.8 g/dL) with normal mean corpuscular volume and elevated LDH (284 U/L). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 116 mm/hour. Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) shows elevated M spike (0.87 g/dL) and λ-light chain restriction (λ 1.42, κ 0.57). Serum immunofixation electrophoresis (SIFE) shows monoclonal IgG λ. Serum free light chain (FLC) shows an elevated λ-light chain (1008 mg/L) and a low κ-light chain (8.96 mg/L). Bone marrow biopsy shows an increase in plasmacytes with a monoclonal expansion of plasma cells. Immunohistochemistry is positive for CD138, lambda light chain, and Ki-67 is 10%. Flow cytometry is positive for CD138, CD56, lambda light chain, and CD28. Diagnosis of multiple myeloma is made, and the patient is started on lenalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone. He is scheduled for stem cell transplant as soon as he is fit.Discussion: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a malignancy of plasma cells that accumulate primarily in the bone marrow. The incidence is around 6 cases per 100,000 people per year and is most common in the elderly, with a median age of diagnosis of 66 years. The etiology of MM is unclear, with both genetic and environmental factors playing a role. MM is more common in males than females, with a 2:1 ratio. Symptoms are often nonspecific and may include fatigue, weakness, weight loss, bone pain, and anemia. Diagnosis of MM requires a biopsy of the bone marrow to show an increase in plasma cells with monoclonal expansion. Staging of MM is done by the International Staging System (ISS), which is based on the serum beta-2 microglobulin and albumin levels at diagnosis. Patients with stage I MM have a normal serum beta-2 microglobulin level and albumin level, while those with stage II MM have an abnormal serum beta-2 microglobulin level but normal albumin level. Stage III MM is characterized by an abnormal serum beta-2 microglobulin level and albumin level. Treatment of MM includes chemotherapy, autologous stem cell transplant, and novel agents such as lenalidomide, bortezomib, and daratumumab. The prognosis of MM is variable and depends on the stage at diagnosis and response to treatment. Survival is around 3-5 years for patients with stage III MM.

Title: Multiple Myeloma and Hypercalcemia: A Case Report

Case: A 59-year-old man presented to the emergency room with generalized weakness and fatigue, along with an inability to ambulate. He reported a 3-day history of intractable nausea and vomiting. He also complained of dysphagia, and he described his urine as darker in color than normal. His medical history included a recent diagnosis of multiple myeloma 4 months prior. He had undergone stem cell transplantation 2 months prior and had been discharged from the hospital 1 month prior, with a planned follow-up visit in 2 weeks. The patient had a family history of multiple myeloma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. He had no history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or kidney disease. On examination, he was cachectic, with a body mass index of 14 kg/m2. He had dry mucus membranes and dry skin. He was dehydrated, with a blood pressure of 140/70 mmHg, a heart rate of 90 beats per minute, and a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute. The patient was alert and oriented. The rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory investigations revealed a serum calcium of 4.85 mmol/L (normal range: 2.10-2.60 mmol/L), a serum phosphorus of 1.10 mmol/L (normal range: 0.81-1.45 mmol/L), a serum albumin of 2.3 g/dL (normal range: 3.4-5.0 g/dL), and a serum creatinine of 2.05 mg/dL (normal range: 0.51-0.94 mg/dL). Serum calcium levels peaked at 4.99 mmol/L on day 2 of admission. Serum creatinine levels peaked at 3.1 mg/dL on day 5 of admission. Other laboratory investigations are shown in Table 1. Serum free light chain testing revealed a monoclonal gammopathy, with a kappa/lambda ratio of 34.04. The patient was diagnosed with multiple myeloma and hypercalcemia. He was treated with intravenous fluids and intravenous bisphosphonates. The patient's hospital course was complicated by renal failure and hypercalcemia-induced cardiac arrhythmias. He was treated with hemodialysis and was discharged from the hospital after his serum calcium levels decreased. He was scheduled for chemotherapy and a bone marrow biopsy to determine the extent of his disease. The patient was followed up in the outpatient clinic 2 months later. His serum calcium levels had decreased to 2.7 mmol/L. His serum creatinine levels had decreased to 1.2 mg/dL. He was scheduled for another cycle of chemotherapy. He was last seen in the clinic 6 months later. He was still undergoing chemotherapy and had a serum calcium of 2.60 mmol/L and a serum creatinine of 1.17 mg/dL. His last cycle of chemotherapy was scheduled for 2 weeks later.

Title: A Case of Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy in a Postmenopausal Woman: A Case Report 
 Introduction: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TCM) is a condition characterized by transient systolic dysfunction of the left ventricle mimicking acute coronary syndrome. It is more common in postmenopausal women and is often associated with severe emotional or physical stress.  Objective: To present a case of TCM in a postmenopausal woman and discuss its clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management.  Case Presentation: A 66-year-old woman with past medical history of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency room with a one-day history of chest pain. The pain was retrosternal, pressure-like in character, and radiating to the jaw and back. It was associated with nausea, vomiting, and diaphoresis. The patient reported feeling overwhelmed and stressed after attending her granddaughter's graduation ceremony the previous day. She denied any history of smoking, family history of coronary artery disease, and prior history of percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass graft surgery. On physical examination, the patient was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg, pulse of 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 100% on room air. Cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm with a grade III/VI systolic murmur heard at the apex. The laboratory workup showed normal troponin I levels and mildly elevated serum creatinine and potassium levels. Electrocardiography (ECG) revealed sinus tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL, V2-V5, and T-wave inversion in leads V5-V6 (Figure 1). Chest X-ray showed no acute cardiac enlargement or pulmonary edema (Figure 2). Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed apical akinesis with an ejection fraction (EF) of 30% and no evidence of valvular abnormalities. The patient underwent a coronary angiogram, which showed normal coronary arteries without any significant stenosis (Figure 3). She was diagnosed with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and was treated with aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, and metoprolol. TTE repeated 48 hours later showed improvement in the EF to 45% (Figure 4). The patient was discharged on aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, and lisinopril.  Discussion: TCM is a reversible cardiomyopathy that typically affects postmenopausal women undergoing severe emotional or physical stress. It is characterized by transient left ventricular dysfunction with apical akinesis and an EF of less than 45%.  It is often referred to as "broken heart syndrome" due to its association with psychosocial stress. The pathophysiology of TCM is not fully understood, but it is believed to be related to catecholamine toxicity and microvascular dysfunction. The presentation of this cardiac condition can be subtle and non-specific, making it a challenge for physicians to diagnose. The aim of this case report is to raise awareness of this condition and provide a brief overview of the clinical presentation, risk factors, and management of TTC in an elderly female patient.

vignettes.prompt: Compose a brief presentation of a patient presenting with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Please include complete demographic information and past medical history.
vignettes.response: Good morning everyone. Today I would like to present a case of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, also known as “broken heart syndrome” is a form of cardiomyopathy that occurs in patients who experience intense physical or emotional stress, particularly women over the age of 50. It is characterized by a sudden onset of chest pain and dyspnea, with ST-segment elevation and transient left ventricular dysfunction. The presentation can be similar to a heart attack, but there is no evidence of coronary artery disease or atherosclerotic plaques. Instead, the left ventricle takes on the shape of a “pot” (Takotsubo in Japanese), with the apex being dilated and the base normal in size. The etiology of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is unknown, but it is thought to be related to a surge of catecholamines released in response to stress. Patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy typically have a good prognosis and recovery is often complete within weeks.

vignettes.response: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TC) is a form of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy that is characterized by regional wall motion abnormalities and typically presents with chest pain and ST-segment elevation on the electrocardiogram (ECG). It has been commonly referred to as “stress cardiomyopathy” or “broken heart syndrome.” TC can be induced by physical or emotional stress and is more common in women than in men. It is important for healthcare providers to be aware of this condition, as the clinical presentation of TC can mimic that of a heart attack, and it is important to differentiate TC from acute coronary syndrome.

vignettes.response: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, also known as broken heart syndrome, is a form of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy that occurs in patients who experience intense physical or emotional stress. The symptoms and signs of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy are similar to those of acute coronary syndrome, including chest pain, dyspnea, and ST-segment elevation on electrocardiogram. However, there are no signs of coronary artery disease or occlusion in these patients. The main characteristic of this syndrome is the presence of a left ventricular apical akinesia with or without regional apical dyskinesia, resembling a “tsunami” shape.

vignettes.response: Introduction: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, also known as stress-induced cardiomyopathy, is a reversible cardiac dysfunction that typically occurs in postmenopausal women. It is characterized by a transient hypokinesis of the apical and mid-ventricular segments of the left ventricle, resulting in a “ball-in-socket” appearance resembling a Japanese octopus trap. The pathophysiology of TCM is not well understood, but it is believed to be related to a catecholamine storm and sympathetic overactivity. TCM is often preceded by physical or emotional stress and can present with chest pain, dyspnea, and electrocardiographic changes. Diagnosis of TCM is based on clinical presentation, electrocardiogram, and echocardiography. Treatment typically involves supportive care, and the prognosis is generally good.

In contrast, the condition is rare in the United States, with an incidence of 0.21 per 100,000 people . However, in recent years, the incidence of TTS has increased in the United States, with an incidence of 1.6 per 100,000 people .

vignettes.response: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (also known as stress-induced cardiomyopathy, broken heart syndrome, or apical ballooning syndrome) is a type of cardiomyopathy that affects the left ventricle of the heart. It is characterized by the appearance of balloon-like changes in the middle and apex of the left ventricle, which resemble a Takotsubo pot used in Japanese cooking. This condition is typically brought on by intense emotional or physical stress and affects postmenopausal women more than men. The symptoms of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy are similar to those of a heart attack, including chest pain, shortness of breath, and nausea. However, unlike a heart attack, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy does not involve a blockage of the coronary arteries. Instead, it is thought to be caused by a surge of catecholamines that lead to abnormal heartbeat patterns and weakening of the heart muscle. Patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy typically recover within a week or two, with no long-term heart damage.

vignettes.response: Hepatitis B is a viral infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which affects the liver. It is a serious condition that can lead to chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. The presentation of hepatitis B can vary from asymptomatic to severe symptoms, including jaundice, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dark urine, and clay-colored stools. The presentation can also vary depending on the stage of the disease, with acute hepatitis B typically presenting with fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal pain, while chronic hepatitis B can be asymptomatic or present with jaundice, fatigue, and weakness. Diagnosis is typically based on blood tests that measure HBV markers, including the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis B surface antibody (HBsAb), hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb), and hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg). Treatment options vary depending on the stage of the disease and include antiviral medications, liver transplant, and vaccination. It is important to note that the hepatitis B virus can be transmitted through blood, semen, and other body fluids, so it is crucial to practice safe sex and take precautions when exposed to blood and bodily fluids to prevent the spread of the virus.

vignettes.response: Title: Successful Management of Acute Hepatitis B in a Renal Transplant Recipient: A Case Report.Author: [Your Name]Abstract: We report a case of acute hepatitis B in a 52-year-old renal transplant recipient who had an uncomplicated hospital course. Our patient was a 52-year-old male who received a kidney transplant in 2002, which was complicated by acute cellular rejection in 2003, 2006, and 2007. He also developed post-transplant diabetes mellitus in 2008. His immunosuppression regimen consisted of mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and prednisone. He presented to the emergency department with a two-week history of progressively worsening abdominal pain. His past medical history was significant for hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and end-stage renal disease secondary to diabetic nephropathy. His family history was negative for liver disease. On admission, he was afebrile, tachycardic, and hypertensive. Physical examination was significant for scleral icterus and tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies revealed an aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 3,132 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 2,848 U/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 128 U/L, total bilirubin of 1.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 0.9 mg/dL, albumin of 3.7 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio (INR) of 1.4. His white blood cell count was 10.9 x 109 cells/L, hemoglobin was 10.7 g/dL, and platelet count was 125 x 109 cells/L. The patient’s hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) was positive, and his HBV DNA was 7.7 log IU/mL. The patient’s hepatitis B core IgG was positive and hepatitis B surface IgG and IgM were negative. He was negative for hepatitis C virus, hepatitis A virus, and cytomegalovirus. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen revealed no evidence of acute cholestatic liver disease or biliary obstruction. The patient was admitted to the medical intensive care unit (ICU) with a diagnosis of acute hepatitis B exacerbation. He was started on lamivudine, which was changed to adefovir dipivoxil due to anemia. His renal function remained stable during his hospitalization. His liver function tests peaked on day three with an AST of 2,150 U/L, ALT of 1,846 U/L, ALP of 125 U/L, total bilirubin of 1.3 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin of 0.9 mg/dL. He was started on intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics due to concern for sepsis. The patient’s clinical status improved, and he was transferred out of the ICU on day four. His liver function tests continued to improve, and he was discharged home on day eight with a plan to follow up as an outpatient.

vignettes.response: Title: A Case of Acute Hepatitis B in a 45-Year-Old Male with No Previous Vaccination for Hepatitis BCase: A 45-year-old male presented to the emergency department complaining of nausea, vomiting, and generalized weakness for one day. He denied any abdominal pain, fever, or chills. He reported having a history of hepatitis B exposure. The patient denied any alcohol consumption. He did not have any history of liver diseases, hepatitis B or C infections, or chronic kidney disease. He reported that he had not been vaccinated against hepatitis B. His family history was significant for diabetes mellitus. On physical examination, the patient was alert and oriented with no signs of jaundice. His vital signs were within normal limits. His abdomen was soft and non-tender without organomegaly. Laboratory tests revealed that the patient was anemic with a hemoglobin level of 11.0 g/dL, elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels of 295 and 251 U/L, respectively, and elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level of 372 U/L. His total bilirubin level was 1.7 mg/dL. His coagulation profile was normal. Urinalysis and urine culture were normal. The patient was diagnosed with acute hepatitis B and was admitted to the hospital. During hospitalization, his liver enzymes and bilirubin levels continued to elevate. He was treated with supportive care, including intravenous fluids and vitamin K. He was also started on acyclovir for possible concurrent viral infection. His symptoms improved, and his liver enzymes and bilirubin levels started to decline after three days of hospitalization. He was discharged on the fourth day with no complications. He was advised to follow up with his primary care provider for further management.Discussion: Acute hepatitis B is an infection of the liver caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV). The virus is transmitted through contact with infected body fluids such as blood and semen. The disease can range from mild to severe, with symptoms such as fatigue, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and yellow eyes. The virus can also cause chronic liver damage, liver cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Hepatitis B is a vaccine-preventable disease, but it remains a significant public health problem worldwide. According to the World Health Organization, approximately 257 million people worldwide are living with chronic hepatitis B infection, and there are an estimated 887,000 new cases of hepatitis B infection each year. In the United States, an estimated 22 million people have been infected with HBV, and 35 million people have been vaccinated against the disease. Hepatitis B is diagnosed through a blood test that detects the presence of the HBV antigens or antibodies. The most common treatment for acute hepatitis B is supportive care, including intravenous fluids and vitamin K. Antiviral medications such as interferon and nucleos(t)ide analogs may be prescribed for severe cases. The disease can take several months to resolve, and the risk of developing chronic liver disease increases with age. Therefore, early diagnosis and treatment are crucial for preventing complications and managing the disease. Prevention through vaccination is also essential, as the vaccine is highly effective in preventing both acute and chronic infections.

vignettes.response: Case Presentation: Patient R.K. is a 58-year-old male who presented to the emergency department on 12/03/2020 with complaints of cough, fever, and sore throat for 7 days. The patient was a former smoker and had a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus. The patient was born in the United States and had no family history of any significant illnesses. Upon arrival, the patient was found to be febrile (102.3°F), tachycardic (100 bpm), and hypoxemic (91%). The patient was given 2 liters of normal saline intravenously, and an arterial line was placed. Laboratory studies were significant for leukocytosis (14.5 K/uL), lymphopenia (0.7 K/uL), elevated ferritin (975 ng/mL), lactate dehydrogenase (666 U/L), and elevated d-dimer (1.3 mg/L). The patient was admitted to the COVID-19 unit and was started on remdesivir, azithromycin, and zinc. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral infiltrates (Figure 1). The patient was placed on a bilevel positive airway pressure (BIPAP) machine for 12 hours, but due to worsening respiratory status, he was intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation. The patient was given methylprednisolone and tocilizumab. On the fourth day of admission, the patient underwent a CT scan of the chest, which revealed ground-glass opacities bilaterally (Figure 2). The patient’s respiratory status continued to worsen, and he was placed on a high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) for 3 days. On the eighth day of admission, the patient developed pulmonary embolism, and enoxaparin was initiated. The patient was placed on a continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) for 2 days due to acute kidney injury. The patient was extubated on the 16th day of admission and transferred to the medical floor. The patient was discharged home after 25 days of hospitalization.

vignettes.response: Title: COVID-19 in a Pregnant Patient with Hypertension and Diabetes.  Medical student level: 3rd year. Learning objectives: 1. To understand the presenting symptoms of COVID-19 in pregnant patients. 2. To review the clinical management of COVID-19 in a pregnant patient. 3. To recognize the need for multidisciplinary care in the management of pregnant patients with COVID-19. Patient demographics: 38-year-old pregnant woman with a past medical history of diabetes and hypertension, gravida 4 para 3 at 36 weeks and 2 days gestation. Patient complaints: fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Findings: The patient was admitted to the hospital with fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Her oxygen saturation was 88% on room air. The patient was diagnosed with COVID-19 and was admitted to the ICU. A chest X-ray was done, which showed bilateral patchy infiltrates. The patient was started on antibiotics and supportive care. The patient's condition deteriorated, and she required invasive mechanical ventilation. The patient was then transferred to the maternity ward for delivery. The patient gave birth to a healthy baby boy with a birth weight of 2.5 kg. The patient was discharged from the hospital after a week. Follow-up: The patient was seen in the follow-up clinic after one month. She was asymptomatic, and her oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. The patient's baby is in good health. Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of recognizing the presenting symptoms of COVID-19 in pregnant patients. It also emphasizes the importance of multidisciplinary care in the management of pregnant patients with COVID-19. The patient was initially managed by the pulmonology team, and then the obstetric team took over her care when she was transferred to the maternity ward for delivery. The patient's obstetrician worked closely with the pediatric team to ensure the best possible care for the patient and her baby. The patient gave birth to a healthy baby boy who is in good health.
